units.tr: Since a community of goods in a well-ordered commonwealth ought neither to be tolerated nor can be tolerated, because the distinction of ownerships was introduced by the law of nations (l. 5 ff. de J. & J.; l. 1 in fin. ff. de furt.; §11 Instit. de rer. div.), and is also approved by divine law (Gen. s. 4 vers. 4; Exod. 20 vers. 5, 17; 1 Corinth. 6 vers. 10; 1 Johan. 3 vers. 17). It seems to stand in the way that c. §8 Resp. pete ex l. 2 §. legis 23 C. de vet. Jur. Enucl., since for settling lawsuits and other very grave causes and reasons, as it were, points with its finger (l. in re 26 ff. de servit. urb. praed.; l. cum pa... 7 §. dulcissimis 20 ff. de Legat. 2). Donellus pursues a similar line in lib. mm. c. 7; Arius Pin. in 2 p. Rubr. (C. de rescind. vend. n. 15 and following, dd. ad l. 42 n. 7 ff. de V.S.); Arum. disp. 4 th. 2; and Lucas Ofiander in his Hir. (Controvers. c. 7), where he answers the arguments of the Anabaptists on the other side. Hence the treatment of the acquisition of ownership is seen to be no small and no lowest part of jurisprudence. Now, this doctrine can conveniently be divided into two main heads: the first will deal with the kinds of ownership, the second with the very modes of acquiring ownership. Of these, the latter is twofold, for ownership is acquired either by the law of nations or by the civil law, and hence the modes of acquiring ownership are of the law of nations or of the civil law (§ sin. Instit. de usu & habit.; l. 1 in pr. ff. de acqu. rer. dom.; §. singulorum Instit. eod., ibid.; Dd.). And although in these texts the interpreters call the modes which we call modes of the law of nations "natural," this is only by reason of the secondary natural law, which is nothing other than the law of nations itself. For that there are no modes of acquiring ownership by purely natural law is clear from this, that the distinction of ownerships is contrary to natural law (junct. l. 4 & s. ff. de J. & J.), and this is taught in plain words in §. singulorum Instit. de rer. div. In this our disputation we shall treat of the modes of acquiring ownership that descend from the law of nations.

units.la: Iure gentium dominia acquiruntur {a} vel per apprehensionem {b} vel per accessionem {c} quarum illa fit seu occupatione {d} quæ aut violenta, & contingit vel venatione {e} vel captura {f} aut non violenta quæ fit vel juven-tione {g} vel traditione {h} Hæc vel confusione {i} vel specificatione {k} seu accessione propriè ita dicta, quæ aut naturalis, aut industrialis. {l}
units.tr: By the law of nations, ownership is acquired {a} either by apprehension {b} or by accession {c}. Of these, the former takes place by occupation {d}, which is either violent and occurs (1) by hunting {e} or (2) by capture {f}; or non-violent, which takes place either (1) by finding {g} or (2) by transfer {h}. The latter is either by confusion {i} or by specification {k}, or by accession properly so called {l}, which is either natural or industrial.

units.la: {a} Tot & nec plures nec pauciores Dominia rerum acquirendi modos Iuris Gentium esse, quam hic a nobis referuntur clarum est ex t, t.Inst.de rer div. & t. t.ff.de acqu.rer.dom. units.tr: {a} That there are as many modes of acquiring ownership of the law of nations as are listed here, and no more and no fewer, is clear from t. t. Inst. de rer. div. and t. t. ff. de acqu. rer. dom. What seems to stand in the way is that in l. in traditionibus C. de pact. only two modes of acquiring ownership are set down, namely traditio and usucapio. Rc.[?] Contius (1 disp. c. 8) holds that the former comprehends all the modes of the civil law, the latter all the modes of the law of nations. Contius (1 disp. 18 in pr. and n. 12), Forc., Neyc. (dial. 84 n. 4), Donell. (4 Comm. 7, etc.), Gom. (r. dn.[?]) and Hackel (illust. qu. disp. 18 th. 1 m. d.) think that all these modes can be included under the two species, apprehension and accession, which we too follow. The interpreters vary on §. singulorum Instit. de rer. div.; Goedd. ad l. rei appellatione 23 n. 4 ff. de V.S.

units.la: {b} In nostra autem distinctione per apprehensionem omnem contractum rerum qui appropriandi animo, vel à nobis, vel ab ijs qui nostra potestati subjecti sunt fieri solet, denotamus.
units.tr: {b} By apprehension, however, in our division we denote every contact of things which is usually made, for the purpose of appropriating them, either by ourselves or by those who are subject to our power.

units.la: {c} Sub accessione v. in genere omne id quod rei nostrae accedit quocunq; modo id fiat comprehendimus.
units.tr: {c} Under accession, in general, we include whatever is added to our thing, in whatever way that comes about.

units.tr: {d} By occupation we mean a contact which depends on our will alone and needs no intervention of an external person. {e} Here we take the word hunting in a general sense, so that it comprehends not only hunting properly so called (which is of four-footed wild beasts in woods and fields) but also fishing and fowling. This is supported by §. feræ igitur Inst. de rer. div. and §. omnia l. 1 ff. de acqu. rer., where it is said: "All animals which are taken in the sky, that is in the air, on the land, in the water, namely wild beasts, fish and birds, become the property of the captors." We call hunting a violent occupation because it is carried out with arms and by pursuit. {f} Although the word capture is so broad in itself that it also embraces hunting, here we take it only for that violent occupation by which we acquire the goods of enemies in war, and we set it apart from hunting. {g} This mode of acquiring is rightly referred to apprehension, and indeed to that apprehension which takes place by occupation. For in finding there is no force; but the taking hold of a thing transfers ownership. Hence if two men see a thing, one first and the other later, and he who saw it later takes it up first, the owner is to be judged not the one who saw it first but the one who first took up the thing lying there (according to the Dd. in l. si Barsatoram §. de fidejus. & mandat.). We rightly call finding a violent occupation, for without arms and noise it cannot be carried out. {h} By transfer we mean a contact or apprehension which cannot be carried out without the intervention and consenting will of some external person. And indeed transfer is rightly placed among the modes of acquisition of the law of nations, by l. qua ratione 9 §. item quoque ff. de acqu. rer. dom., §. per traditionem Instit. de rer. div.; Ulpian seems to say so in Frag. c. 19, and see Wesemb. ad §. 2 Instit. de tamen. ordin., and Fomannus, who followed him, disp. 9 th. 26 m. 1, who hold that these are carried out by apprehension. For true traditio is nothing without apprehension (l. traditionibus C. de pact.; l. serv. C. de rei vind.). In traditio, for the transfer of ownership, the apprehension of the body is required, and besides this an empty offering of possession is not necessary, as the Dd. and the gloss on l. si agerf. de rei vind. agree (per §. per traditionem Instit. de rer. div.; l. 20 ff. de acqu. rer. dom.; arg. l. naturaliter 12 ff. de acqu. poss.), which Castrensis follows on l. 2 de act. Empt., and Donellus (4 Comm. 19). Contra: Contius (1 disp. 8), Wesemb. in parat. de contrah. empt., Hottom. (illustr. quaest. 11), Mynsinger (1 obs. 53), by l. cum res 12 C. de probat., qui praedium 13 C. de distract. pignor., l. 2 §. 1, §. 2 C. de act. empt., and 18 de vi et vi armata. Yet traditio can be made without apprehension (§. interdum Instit. de rer. div.), the reason for which Wesemb. and Baro give there. {i} Although the interpreters subtly distinguish between confusion and commixture, holding that confusion is of liquid things and of those which can hardly be separated, and commixture of dry things and of those which can easily be separated (fundament. §. 22 and following, Instit. de rer. div.), nevertheless, since these words are very often confused, as can be seen from Pomponius in pr. junct. sed si plumbum ff. de rei vind., we here use the broader meaning and take the words as one and the same. {k} Goedd. thinks (p. 3 disp. 3 th. fin.) that specification also takes place by confusion, and that confusion is comprehended under it. But these are very different things: confusion is said to occur when different bodies, or bodies of different matter, are mixed so that they do not make one body or one new species, but remain different bodies; whereas specification is called the case when different species are mixed so that they make a new species different from the former. Accordingly, if the word specification is taken very broadly and improperly, we admit Goedd.'s opinion; but if it is taken strictly and properly, we cannot admit it. {l} By accession properly so called, which we understand as that which is added to our thing but does not so combine with it that together with our thing it forms either one species or one confused body, we divide it into natural and industrial (argum. §. item ea cum §§ seqq., junct. §. cum in suo §§ qq. Instit. de rer. div.). Concerning this accession, specifically so called, see Pecki-

units.la: Venatio non quidem animalia Cicura {b} attamen ias feras semper {c} Cicuritas ac mansuefactas tum si[?] fuetudinem redeundi deferunt {d} sive in proprio, sive lieno fundo captae, capientium dominio subjicit, in um ut quam diu sub potestate nostra sunt, nostri do-ij esse judicentur.
units.tr: Hunting does not indeed extend to tame animals, but it does extend to wild beasts, which, though they are always of a tame and domesticated disposition, still keep the habit of returning. When they are taken on one's own land or another's, the captor's dominion subjects them to himself, so that for as long as they are in our power they are judged to be ours.

units.la: (a) Quomodo per venationem quid acquirere possimus, ut eò us intelligatur distinctionem quandam animalium instituere. Sciendum igitur ex distinctione ad I.C. pertinente, animalia esse ferae, vel Cicura, vel Cicurata. Fera animalia dicuntur quae o-ò indomitae sunt naturae, & in sylvis, campis ac aquis degunt, ut generis cervi, lepores, ursi, leones, grues, vultures, Phasiani, [?]ures, pisces, castores, mergi, &c. quibus etiam annumerantur apes §. apium quoque Instit. de rer. div. quod tamen de apibus allonon inclusis accipiendum putamus, cum quo convenit Ius Saxonicum, quod omnia illa animalia fera naturae facit, quae à pastoribus durinequeunt gloss. Landrecht lib. 2. art. 40. Cicura & mansuetae domi nobiscum in nostris fundis habentur ut boves equi, gallinae, anseres, quarum duorum ultimarum specierum non sed mansuetam naturam esse inde arguit Imper. Justinianus dentur gallinae ferae & anseres feri §. Gallinarum Instit. de rer. divis.
units.tr: (a) To see how we can acquire something by hunting, we must first draw a certain distinction among animals. It should be known, then, from the distinction that belongs to the jurists, that animals are either wild (ferae), tame (cicura), or tamed (cicurata). Wild animals are those of untamed nature that live in woods, fields and waters, such as deer, hares, bears, lions, cranes, vultures, pheasants, [?]ures, fish, beavers, mergansers, and so on. Bees are also counted among them (§ apium quoque, Inst. de rer. div.), though we think this must be understood of bees not enclosed in hives. The Saxon law agrees, and it makes wild by nature all those animals that cannot be driven by herdsmen (gloss, Landrecht lib. 2, art. 40). Tame and gentle animals are kept with us at home on our estates, such as oxen, horses, hens and geese. That the last two kinds are of gentle nature and not wild, the emperor Justinian argues from the fact that wild hens and wild geese are mentioned (§ Gallinarum, Inst. de rer. div.).

units.la: Cicurata seu mansuefacta animalia vocantur quae naturaliter em fera natura sunt, sed accidentaliter hominum industria & intentia mansueta sunt reddita: cujus generis opinione J.C. §. pavonem quoque columbas pavones cervi mansuefacti, & id genus alia. Quibus nos quoq; apes alveis inclusos annumerandos putamus, quod eos in alvearia vel arborem includendo quis & cicurare suos facere dicatur arg. d. §. pavonum quoque & arg. l. 3. §. qui-ectè 16, ff. de acquir. poss. etiam de jure Saxon. gloss Weichbilde 120.
units.tr: Tamed or domesticated animals are those which are wild by nature but have been made gentle by human effort and management. Of this kind, in the jurists' opinion, are peacocks, doves, tamed deer, and others of that sort (§ pavonem quoque, Inst. de rer. div.). We think that bees enclosed in hives should be counted with them as well, since one who encloses them in a hive or tree is said to tame them and make them his own (arg. d. § pavonum quoque, and arg. l. 3, § qui ... 16, ff. de acquir. poss.; also Saxon law, gloss Weichbild 120).

units.la: Nam licet hoc & ejusmodi alia animalia à Justiniano §.api§.apium quoque & §.pavonum quoque Instit.de rer.div. fera natura esse dicantur, eadem tamen fera cicurata & mansuefacta esse ipsa verba hor.text.ut & l.37.ff.de furt. luculentissimè ostendunt (b) Animalia Cicura per venationem nullo modo occupari, sed à domino quocunq; loco vindicari possunt, in tantum ut in eadem restituere recusantem domino detur furti actio etiam pro gallina unica §.gallinarum Instit.de rer.div. Nec obstat quod cum de minimis non curet prætor, ob rem tam parvi momenti furti actio non institui posse, videatur: furti enim actio non ex re subtracta, sed ex qualitate facti astimanda est. Nec etiam obstat, quod doli actio non competat de minori summa duobus aureis l 4.C.de restit.in integr. dolus enim præsentis cum quo contrahimus facilius præcaveri potest quam ignoti furtum, ut ita dispar hic subsit ratio. Taceo quod doli actio sit extraordinaria & proinde de re minima non detur, fundani.l. scio 4 ff. de in integr.restit. furti verò actio sit ordinaria quam responsionem habet Myns.in §.gallinarum n.1.hic. De jure Saxon. possum gallinas alienis domum meam involantibus ibiq; damnum dantibus alas amputare,easq; domum remittere Weichbild art.111.Si verò eas occi-dero teneor solvere pro gallinis singulis dimidium solidum Lantrecht[?] lib.3.art.51.(c) Ex animalibus ea quae omninò feræ natura existunt, venari de jure gentium Civium licitum est, in tantum ut contra me in fundo venari prohibentem actionem injuriarum habeam l.13.ff. de injurijs ex ea ratione quod sicut aqua profluens, & aer quo ad proprietatem nullius sint in bonis §.& quidem Instit.de rer.div. Sic & animalia in aere (in quo degere ferae quoq; rectius dicuntur, nec solo cohaerere secundum gloss. in l.sin. vero quasi vento C.de alim.pupill. præstand.) ac aqua degentia rectè nullius censentur, proindeq; occupanti cedant §.all.ferae igitur & §.apium Instit.de rer div. Et hoc in tantum procedit, ut aves & terrestria animalia quod concernit, non modo meum proprium, sed & alienum fundum venandi, & aucupandi gratia ingredi all.§.ferae & §.apium l.3,ff.de acqui.rer.dom. & proinprindè ipes quoq; cum feri vermes sint alveũ non inclusas ex alieno fundo capere possim d. §.apium, & quicquid ita pervenationem capio meum efficit, modo illud ceperim non n. persecutio, ut nec vulneratio; sed captura feram efficit §. illud quæsitum d.loc.l. f.§.illud quæsitum ff.cod. meumq; manet tam diu, quam diu id in potestate mea, vel ego illud persecutione mea recuperare possim illudq; postquam aufugit persequor, persecutione vero mea cessante vel animali in tali statu posito ut recuperare difficillime illud possim naturali libertati restitutum censetur, & occupanti cedit §. ferae cum §§. seqq. duob.Inst.de rer. divis.l.f.in pr.§.1.ff.de acq.rer.dom. Fera enim non censentur fructus fundi, sed in eo libere vagantur fundumq; pro libitu relinquere possunt l.3.§. item fera> ff.de acq. rer. dom. Wesemb. in parat.ff. de acq.rer.dom.n.7. Fera tamen animalia tam terrestria tam volatilia alicujus vivario inclusa inde citra furtum eximi non possunt, quia in privati possessione & quodammodo fructus fundi existunt d.§.item feras cum §.seq. Licet autem in fundo alieno ve- nari possim, nec in venationem actione ulla conuenire possim: tamen is cui fundus est potest prohibere, ne venandi aut aucupandi aut mel ac apes auferendi causa ipsius fundum ingrediar. & si contra hanc prohibitionem facio, habet in me actionem injuriarum all. §. feræ & §. apium l. 16. ff. de servit. rustic. præd. non tamen sic contra prohibitionem capta dominus fundi; sed venator acquirit §. feræ instit. d. lo. l. in laqueum 15. ff. de acqu. rer. dom. l. agrum C. de servit. & aqua; & si tali modo omnibus in meo fundo venari interdico illiq; per tempus immemoriale acquiescunt, hoc ipso mihi jus proprium ac tale acquisitum ut nemo posteà in meo fundo venari possit cum tali præscriptione in fi ar privilegij fit l. 1. 2. ac 11. C. de servit. & aqua l. 3. §. ductus aquæ C. de aqua quotid. & æstiv. & me non minus ac lex seu consuetudo in meo jure firmet c super quibusdam §. præterea de V.S. Wesen. b. in parat. ff. de acq. rer. dom. n. 7. Et tali modo acquisiverunt principes venationes in plerisq; [illegible, ~3 letters] fibiq; eisdem quasi proprias dicarunt, in tantum ut hodie non modo in publicis; sed & in privatis fundis ac me[ribus] easdem privatis rectè interdicere possint: subditi enim dum acquieverunt in factà prohibitione principes, aliosq; prohibentes in ure venationum ita firmarunt, ut hodie nemo subditorum seu privatorum, venatione uti possit, nisi qui vel similiter per tempus immemoriale non modò utendo, sed & alios prohibendo hac venationum jura sibi acquisivit l. si quisquam ff. de diverf. temp. praescript. vel cui hoc speciatim à principibus indultum. Nec refert quod inferri possit, principium hujus praescriptionis vitiosum esse, quia prohibitio venationum est contra libertatem naturalem: nam patientia subditorum hunc titulum & initium sufficienter & ita purgat, ut hi non modò in acquisitionem consentire, sed & venationum jura ad praescriptionem eorundem tacentes principibus quasi motu proprio deferre videantur.
units.tr: For although Justinian says that this animal and others of its kind are of wild nature (§ apium quoque and § pavonum quoque, Inst. de rer. div.), the very words of that passage and of l. 37, ff. de furt., show most clearly that these same wild animals, once tamed and domesticated, are tame. Tame animals cannot be acquired by hunting in any way, but the owner may claim them from any place, so that an action for theft is given against one who refuses to restore them to the owner, even for a single hen (§ gallinarum, Inst. de rer. div.). Nor does it stand in the way that, since the praetor does not concern himself with trifles, an action for theft seems not to lie for a thing of so small value. For the action for theft is judged not by the thing taken but by the nature of the act. Nor does it stand in the way that an action for fraud does not lie for a sum under two gold pieces (l. 4, C. de restit. in integr.). For fraud by a present party with whom we contract can more easily be guarded against than theft by an unknown person, so the reason here is different. I pass over the point that the action for fraud is extraordinary and so is not given for a trifling matter (Fundanius, l. Scio 4, ff. de in integr. restit.), whereas the action for theft is ordinary and has its own remedy (Mynsinger, in § gallinarum n. 1, hic). By Saxon law I may cut off the wings of hens that fly into my house from others' land and do damage there, and send them home (Weichbild art. 111). But if I kill them, I am bound to pay half a shilling for each hen (Landrecht lib. 3, art. 51). (c) Of animals, those that are wild by nature altogether may be hunted by citizens under the law of nations, to such an extent that against one who forbids me to hunt on his land I have an action for injury (l. 13, ff. de injuriis). The reason is that, just as flowing water and air belong to no one as property (§ et quidem, Inst. de rer. div.), so animals living in the air (in which wild creatures are more correctly said to dwell, not clinging to the ground, according to the gloss on l. sin. vero, quasi vento, C. de alim. pupill. praest.) and in water are rightly held to belong to no one, and so pass to whoever takes them (§ ferae igitur, § apium, Inst. de rer. div.). This goes so far that, as regards birds and land animals, I may enter not only my own estate but also another's for the sake of hunting and fowling (all. § ferae and § apium; l. 3, ff. de acq. rer. dom.). Therefore I may also take wild bees from another's land, since they are wild creatures, if they are not enclosed in a hive (d. § apium). Whatever I take by hunting becomes mine: it is not the pursuit or the wounding, but the capture that makes the wild animal mine (§ illud quaesitum, d. loc.; l. f. § illud quaesitum, ff. cod.). It remains mine as long as it is in my power, or as long as I can recover it by pursuit, and I pursue it when it has escaped. But when my pursuit ceases, or the animal is placed in such a state that I can recover it only with the greatest difficulty, it is deemed restored to natural liberty and passes to whoever takes it (§ ferae, with the following §§, two Inst. de rer. div.; l. f. in pr. and § 1, ff. de acq. rer. dom.). For wild animals are not counted as fruits of the estate; they roam freely in it and may leave the estate at will (l. 3, § item fera, ff. de acq. rer. dom.; Wesenbeck, in parat. ff. de acq. rer. dom. n. 7). Yet wild animals, whether land or flying, enclosed in a fishpond or aviary, cannot be removed from there without theft, because they are in private possession and in a way are fruits of the estate (d. § item feras, with the following §). Although I may hunt on another's estate and cannot be sued for hunting there, the owner of the estate can nevertheless forbid me to enter it for the purpose of hunting, fowling, or taking honey and bees. If I act against this prohibition, he has an action for injury against me (all. § ferae and § apium; l. 16, ff. de servit. rustic. praed.). But the owner does not thereby acquire what is taken against the prohibition; the hunter acquires it (§ ferae, Inst. d. loc.; l. in laqueum 15, ff. de acq. rer. dom.; l. agrum, C. de servit. et aqua). If in this way I forbid everyone to hunt on my estate, and they acquiesce for immemorial time, I thereby acquire for myself a right of this kind, so that afterwards no one may hunt on my estate. Such a prescription takes the place of a privilege (l. 1, 2 and 11, C. de servit. et aqua; l. 3, § ductus aquae, C. de aqua quotid. et aestiv.), and the law or custom confirms it in my right no less (c. super quibusdam, § praeterea, de V.S.; Wesenbeck, in parat. ff. de acq. rer. dom. n. 7). In this way princes have acquired the hunting rights in many places and claimed them for themselves as if they were their own. Hence today they may rightly forbid hunting not only on public lands but also on private estates, and [illegible] to private persons. For subjects, by acquiescing in the prohibitions imposed by princes and in the forbidding of others, have so firmly established these hunting rights that today none of the subjects or private persons may hunt, unless he has acquired these hunting rights for himself in the same way over immemorial time, by using them and also by forbidding others, or unless it has been granted to him specifically by the princes (l. si quisquam, ff. de diversis temporalibus praescriptionibus). Nor does it matter that it may be objected that the beginning of this prescription is flawed, because the prohibition of hunting is against natural liberty. For the patience of the subjects sufficiently cleanses this title and beginning, so that they appear not only to have consented to the acquisition but also, by their silent acquiescence in the prescription, to have handed over the rights of hunting to the princes, as if of their own accord.

units.tr: Capture: persons and goods taken in a just war are adjudged to the captors.

units.la: Ut in venatione, sic & captivitate res nostro dominio subjicimus §.item ea Instit.de rer.div.l.adeo in pr.ff.de acqu.rer.dom.l.1.§.1.ff.de acqu.poffeff. modo bellum justum fit h e.tale quod a populo Roma-no aliis, vel ab alii\, populoRomano indictum, vel inter eos, qui su-periorem non recognoscunt, geritur, hi enim hostes proprie dicun-tur, ceteri prædones l.hostes ff.de captiv.& postlim. reverf.l. hostes ff. de V.S.& quidem personæ & res mobiles in bello captæ militum ca-pientium fiunt d.§,modo non obstet mos vel pactum: Ex nonnulla-rum enim gentium belligerantium more vel pactis captivi [illegible, ~10 letters] so-luto liberi fiunt. Res immobiles vero belli duci, vel populo qui bel-lum gerit, acquiruntur l.captivus ff.de captiv.& postlim reverf. Si ita-men in bello capta nostra potestati eximuntur similiter ut fera capta nostra esse desinunt d.§.item ea quæ ex hostibus.
units.tr: As in hunting, so also in captivity we bring things under our dominion. Provided the war is just, that is, one waged by the Roman people against others, or by others against the Roman people, or between those who recognise no superior. For these are properly called enemies; the rest are pirates. Persons and movable things taken in war become the property of the soldiers who capture them, provided no custom or agreement stands in the way. For under the custom or agreements of some belligerent nations, captives become free once the ransom is paid. Immovable things, however, are acquired by the commander of the army or by the people who wage the war. If, however, things taken in war are released from our power, they cease to be ours in the same way that a captured wild animal does.
