units.la: Inventione acquirimus vel res, quæ nondum in alicujus dominio fuerunt{a} vel res pro derelicto habitas,{b} vel thesaurum{c}.
units.tr: We acquire by finding things that have not yet been in anyone's ownership, or things regarded as abandoned, or treasure.

units.la: {a} (a) Pro rebus quæ nondum in alicujus dominio fuerunt ha-bentur bentur gemmæ, lapides Margaritæ (quæ Species quomodo invicem differant de eo consule l. fi non sunt §. sin.ff.de auro & argent. legat. ubi dicitur,quod gemmæ sint materia pellucida,& gemma quasi gemma nominentur, quam Etymologiam improbat Laurent. Valla lib.6.elegant.c.ult.) aliaq; in maris litore n.isfcentia.Hac omnia similiter ut mare jure naturali omnibus communia sunt: prinde q; cum in nullius dominio existant,occupanti cedunt §.item lapilli Institt. de rer.div.(b)Hoc item modo acquiruntur res pro derelicto habita §.qua ratione Institt.eod.l.1.ff.pro derelicto. Dicuntur autem res pro derelicto habita ,quas dominus ita abjicit,ut earsdem in rebus suis amplius habere noluerit §.all.unde illa res que in tempestate à nautis levandæ navis erat ejiciuntur §.alia sane sin.Institt.eod.l.2. in sin. l. 8.ff.ad L.Rhod.de jact.l.9.§.alia ff.de acqu.rer.dom.l.21.§.1.ff.de acqu. possunt vel incendij causa projiciuntur l.1.ff.de incend.ruin.&nauf.vel erbeda currenti ignerantibus domini decidunt §.all. alia l 43.§. qui alienum ff.de furt. vel aliàs amittuntur §.alia Inst.de rer.div.Cum nõ abjiciendi,sed majoris piculi evitâdi causâ relinquantur,pro derelicto nõ suat habende,hinc non fiunt occupantis, sed legitimo domino sub pœna furti sunt reftitueda jurib.all.d.l.falsus creditor §.qui alienum quid & §.proinde ff.de fugt. 'De jure quoq; Saxonico, rem alienam inveniens,vel à latronibus ac furibus recuperans,vel fi domino rei eandem petente fe eam habere negat,vel si non notum facit edicto publico , quod hanc rem alienam secum habeat furtum committit: non tamen ordinaria pœna furti puniri potest in differ. Zob. à Romanedittis part.2.diff.61.Sabiniani tamen existimarunt, nautas in naufragiis res ejectas pro derelicto habere,eo quod ex duobus unum eligant,& in ipsam jacturam rei consentiant l. falsus 43. §. qui alienum cum §.seq.& §.pen.ult.ff.de furt. id enim necessitate compulsi faciunt naut.e,in necessariis autem nemo liberalitatem exercere præsumatur, & hæc Sabinianorum jàdudum explosa est sententia per contraria responsa l.qui levandæ 8.l.2.in sin ff.ad L.Rhod. de jact. §. act. §. alia sanè Instit. de rer. div.& constitutionem novam authent, quo jure novissimo res naufragorum surripientium bona fisco adju-dicantur, non obstante contraria consuetudine auth. navigia C. de furt. Si tamen nautæ animo rem derelinquendi jactum faciunt, res sic derelictas occupantibus fieri non negamus, sed potius cum Ulp. & Sabiniani in d.l. falsus §. quod si dominus & §. si jactum ff. de furt. affirmamus, quæ voluntas nautarum unde elici possit eleganter explicat Conanus lib.3.c.3. & Menoch. lib.5. præsumpt 30. Illud hîc ab interpretibus investigari solet. ◊An inventor ob restitutionem suctam premium exigere possit? Negativa verior videtur per d.l. falsus §. ergo ff. de furt. Schneidvv tamen in §.sin.Inst.de rer.div. hanc opinionem limitat, quod inventor pro oper. rei conquirendæ causâ adhibita licitè præmium petat, quod Jacob. de Bellovifo lib. 1.c.10. n.54. pract.Criminal. ampliat dicendo inventorem posse uti retentione donec de interesse satisfiat. De jure Saxonum rem alienam inveniens publico edicto ex cathedra ecclesiæ notificare debet, si hanc rem invenisse. Publico hoc edicto facto si dominus rei intra sex septimanas sese sistit, si ejusmodi cum inventore est territorii rem libere ac totaliter recuperat: Si verò extraneus potest inventor tertiam sibi partem præmij loco retinere. Quod si se non sistit intra sex septimanas res illa pro duab. partibus judici istius loci, tertia inventori cedit. Sander.[?] lib.2.art.37
units.tr: {a} (a) Things regarded as not yet in anyone's ownership include gems, stones, pearls (on how these species differ from one another, consult l. fi non sunt §. sin. ff. de auro & argento legato, where it is said that gems are a transparent matter and are named gemma as if gemma, an etymology that Laurentius Valla rejects, Elegantiae lib. 6, c. ult.), and other things found on the seashore. All of these, like the sea itself, are common to all by the law of nature, and therefore, since they belong to no one, they go to whoever takes them into possession: §. item lapilli, Inst. de rer. div. (b) In the same way, things regarded as abandoned are acquired: §. qua ratione, Inst. eod.; l. 1 ff. pro derelicto. Things are said to be regarded as abandoned when the owner casts them off in such a way that he no longer wishes to have them among his possessions: §. alii, Inst. eod.; for example, those things which are thrown overboard by sailors to lighten the ship in a storm: §. alia sane, sin. Inst. eod.; l. 2 in fin.; l. 8 ff. ad L. Rhod. de jact.; l. 9 §. alia ff. de acq. rer. dom.; l. 21 §. 1 ff. de acq. poss. Or they may be thrown out to prevent a fire, l. 1 ff. de incend. ruin. & naufrag.; or they may fall into the sea without the knowledge of their owners, §. alii, and l. 43 §. qui alienum ff. de furt.; or they may be lost in other ways, §. alia, Inst. de rer. div. Since such things are left not with the intention of abandoning them but to avoid a greater danger, they are not to be regarded as abandoned; hence they do not become the property of the one who takes them, but must be restored to the lawful owner under penalty of theft: d. l. falsus creditor; §. qui alienum quid & §. proinde ff. de furt. Also under Saxon law, one who finds another's property, or recovers it from robbers and thieves, and then denies having it when the owner seeks it, or does not make public by public edict that he has the property of another, commits theft; yet he cannot be punished with the ordinary penalty for theft: see Zoesius, De Romanis edictis, part 2, diff. 61. The Sabinians, however, thought that sailors regard goods thrown overboard in a shipwreck as abandoned, because they choose one of two evils and consent to the loss itself: l. falsus 43 §. qui alienum cum §. seq. & §. pen. ult. ff. de furt. For they do this compelled by necessity, and no one is presumed to exercise generosity in necessary matters. But this opinion of the Sabinians was long ago rejected by contrary responses: l. qui levandæ 8; l. 2 in fin. ff. ad L. Rhod. de jact.; §. actio; §. alia sane, Inst. de rer. div.; and by a new constitution (authentic), by which the goods of shipwrecked persons that are stolen are adjudged to the fisc, notwithstanding a contrary custom: auth. navigia C. de furt. If, however, sailors throw goods overboard with the intention of abandoning them, we do not deny that such goods, once abandoned, become the property of those who take them; indeed, we affirm this with Ulpian and the Sabinians in d. l. falsus, §. quod si dominus, and §. si jactum ff. de furt. The will of the sailors, from which it may be inferred, is elegantly explained by Conanus, lib. 3, c. 3, and Menochius, lib. 5, præsumpt. 30. Here the commentators usually inquire: ◊ Can the finder demand a reward for the restoration he has made? The negative seems more correct, according to d. l. falsus §. ergo ff. de furt. Schneidewin, however, on §. sin. Inst. de rer. div., limits this opinion, holding that the finder may lawfully claim a reward for the effort he has spent in searching for the thing; Jacobus de Belvisio, lib. 1, c. 10, n. 54, Pract. Criminal., extends this by saying that the finder may use retention until he is satisfied for his interest. By the law of the Saxons, one who finds another's property must notify it by public edict from the pulpit of the church that he has found it. If, after this public edict, the owner of the thing presents himself within six weeks, and he is of the same territory as the finder, he recovers the thing freely and wholly. If, however, the claimant is a stranger, the finder may keep a third part of the reward for himself. But if the owner does not present himself within six weeks, that thing goes two parts to the judge of that place and one third to the finder. Sander[?], lib. 2, art. 37.

units.la: (c) Tertio per inventionem acquiritur thesaurus h.e. antiquitus depositæ pecuniæ cujus non extat memoria, quæ dominum non habet l. nunquam nuda §.1.ff. de acq. rer.dom. cujus consilarium[?] tam pecuniam cujus depositorem probabiliter scire possumus, non thesaurum esse, & proinde inventam non inventori cedere, sed deponentis ejusdem hæredum manere l. nunquam §.fi in sin. & l. peregrè ff. de acq. poss. Hinc pecunia inventa in re empta non in modum thesauri; sed E.C. quod à venditoris parentibus ibi depositæ sit non ad emptorem, sed venditorem totaliter pertinet ut est text. form. in l. nunquam §.1,ff. de acqu. rer.dom. l. peregrè ff. de acqu. poss. l. à tu-tore tore ff. de rei vind. vide Alvarot. in c.1. n.8. quæ sint regalia in ufib. Feu-dor. Sunt autem certa requisita quæ intervenire debent, ad id, ut thesaurum inventum quis suum faciat, ad hæc intelligenda sequentes assertiones sunt notanda. 1. Si investigatur & invenitur thesaurus magicus, & aliis illicitis, sive in suo sive in alieno loco non inventori sed fisco applicatur l.unic. in pr. C. de thesauris, quia rei illicitæ operam dans inde commodum sperare non debet. 2. Si invenitur in fundo, vel alio loco proprio fit inventoris §. thesauros Instit. de rer. div. idq; ex præscripto Divi Hadriani d. l. unic. C. de Thesaur. 3. Si invenitur in loco alieno data operâ, cedit totus non inven-tori, sed loci domino: non enim licitum est in alterius fundo thesaurum inquirere d.l.un. C. de thesaur. 4. Si invenitur in loco alieno casu & fortuitò dimidius inventori, & dimidius loci domino applicatur, nec refert locus publicus an privatus sit. In privato ergo loco alieno inventus dimidius inventori, dimidius domino illius loci privati applicatur. In loco cæsaris patrimoniali vel publico fiscali invento dimidius inventori, dimidius fisco. Cæsaris in pædia all §. thes [illegible, ~40 letters] faurus l.3.§.penult.ff.de jur.fisci. Illud quæstionis est in loco sacro vel religioso fortuitò inventus,cui cedat? Hoc enim in punct.d.§ penult. l.3,ff.de jurefisci §.thesauros Instit.de rer.div.& c.unic.quæ sint res regal.in usib.feud discrepantia habemus jura. Nec enim Hotm.We-semb.ad §.thesauros Instit.de rer,div.&Borcholt.in c.unic. quæ sint regal.in usib.feudor.sententiam approbare possumus,qui nullam hic courtuoniap d.ari existimant §.thesauros d.loc.sacr.& religiosis privatis §.si in locis l.3.ad c.unic.de locis sacris ac religiosis publicis seu fiscalib.interpretantur. Eam ergò horum text.genuinam interpretationem esse existimamus.D.fratres primum ut in loco sacro & religioso casu inventus thesarus, dimidius fisco Imperatoris cederet voluerunt d.l.3.§.penult, idque non sine ratione; sed ex illo æquitatis capite,quod loca religiosa fisci imperatorij sint. D. Hadrianus vero naturalem æquitatem secutus in loco sacro & religioso fortuitò inventum[?] ventum thesaurum totum inventori assignavit. Postea Justinianus Imper. in §. thesauros Instit.de rer.div. non Divor.fratrum ut Duar. in tit.de solut.matrim.column.1.in sin.&ad tit.de acq.rer.dom. c.4. & Donell.4.Comm.14.existimant,sed D. Hadriani sententiam approbavit,ut recte sentit Godefrid.Novell.Leonis 51.eumq.secutus Fornannus disp.Inst.9.th.8.lit.h.Deinde Fridericus Imp.repudiata Justiniani & Hadriani sententia D.fratrum opinionem revocavit,& in forum reduxit c.unic.quae sint regal.in usib.feudor. Verum hisce iurib.omnib.derogatur putant Dd.dum ex notatis in c.1. de sent.& rejudic. ubi traditur: quod loca sacra & religiosa in dominio superioris ecclesiae esse dicantur, concludunt dimidiam partem thesauri in loco religioso inventi inventori,dimidiam praelato tribuendam esse. Verum hodie in praxi non attenta hac Dd.opinione sententiam D.fratrum & c.unic.observari,censemus. Illud hic quod quaestionis est. An inventus thesaurus vel pro rei circumstantia ejus dimidiatus in fundo cujus dominium divisum directo an utili domino puta vasallo & usufructuario acquiratur? ad dominum directum seu proprietatis talem thesaurum pertinere existimamus l.divortio §.si fundum in sin.ff.solu.matrim.Et in hoc quoq; convenit Jus Saxon.cum Jur.Civ.ut ostendit Wesemb.in not.ad §.Instit.de rer.div.& Heig.in §.39.Instit.eod.fundam.constit.Electi.53.p.2. non obstante text.Landrecht/lib.1.art.35. Alle Schätze unter der Erde begraben tieffer denn ein Pflug/gehören zu der königlichen Gewalt. Nam licet illud olim sic in usu fuerit, hodie tamen hic text.de metallicis venis intelligendus est, ut declarant Dd. praecitati loc.fund.cit.constit.53.
units.tr: (c) Thirdly, treasure is acquired by finding, that is, money long ago deposited whose memory has perished and which has no owner: l. nunquam nuda §. 1 ff. de acq. rer. dom. Yet where we can probably know the depositor of the money, it is not treasure, and so what is found does not pass to the finder but remains with the heirs of that depositor: l. nunquam §. fin. in fin. and l. peregrè ff. de acq. poss. Hence money found in a purchased thing, not in the manner of treasure, but which was deposited there by the parents of the seller, belongs wholly not to the buyer but to the seller, as the text in the form of l. nunquam §. 1 ff. de acq. rer. dom. and l. peregrè ff. de acq. poss. and l. a tutore ff. de rei vind. show. See Alvarotus on c. 1, n. 8, Quæ sint regalia in usibus feudorum. Certain requisites must concur for someone to make found treasure his own, and in understanding these, the following propositions are to be noted. 1. If magical treasure, or treasure sought by other unlawful means, is searched for and found, whether on one's own or another's ground, it is applied to the fisc and not to the finder, l. unic. in pr. C. de thesauris, because one who works at an unlawful thing should not hope to gain any benefit from it. 2. If it is found in a field or other place that belongs to the finder, it is his: §. thesauros, Inst. de rer. div., and this in accordance with the prescription of the Divine Hadrian, d. l. unic. C. de thesaur. 3. If it is found in another's place by deliberate search, the whole goes not to the finder but to the owner of the place, for it is not lawful to seek treasure in another's field: d. l. unic. C. de thesaur. 4. If it is found by chance and accident in another's place, one half goes to the finder and one half to the owner of the place; nor does it matter whether the place is public or private. Therefore in a private place of another, what is found is divided: half to the finder, half to the owner of that private place. In a place of the emperor's patrimony or a public fiscal place, what is found goes half to the finder and half to the fisc. Imperial, in pædia all §. thes[illegible]aurus l. 3 §. penult. ff. de jure fisci. The question arises: to whom does treasure found by chance in a sacred or religious place belong? For on this point, in d. §. penult. l. 3 ff. de jure fisci, §. thesauros Inst. de rer. div., and c. unic. quæ sint res regal. in usibus feudorum, we have conflicting laws. Nor can we approve the opinion of Hotman on §. thesauros Inst. de rer. div., or of Borcholten on c. unic. quæ sint regalia in usibus feudorum, who think there is no controversy here at all, and who interpret the §. thesauros as dealing with sacred and religious places that are private, and §. si in locis, l. 3 ad c. unic. de locis sacris ac religiosis, as dealing with public or fiscal ones. We therefore consider this to be the genuine interpretation of these texts. The Divine Brothers first wished that treasure found by chance in a sacred and religious place should go half to the fisc of the emperor: d. l. 3 §. penult., and not without reason, but from that principle of equity, that religious places are the property of the imperial fisc. The Divine Hadrian, however, following natural equity, assigned the whole treasure found by chance in a sacred and religious place to the finder. Afterwards the Emperor Justinian, in §. thesauros Inst. de rer. div., approved not the opinion of the Divine Brothers (as Duarenus on tit. de solutione matrimonii, col. 1 in fin., and on tit. de acq. rer. dom. c. 4, and Donellus, 4 Comm. 14, think), but the opinion of the Divine Hadrian, as Godefridus rightly thinks on Novel. Leonis 51, and Fornanus, following him, Disp. Inst. 9, th. 8, lit. h. Next, the Emperor Frederick, rejecting the opinions of Justinian and Hadrian, revoked the opinion of the Divine Brothers and restored it to use: c. unic. quæ sint regal. in usibus feudorum. But the doctors think that all these laws are derogated, since from what is noted in c. 1 de sent. & re judicata, where it is taught that sacred and religious places are said to be in the dominion of the superior church, they conclude that half of the treasure found in a religious place should be given to the finder and half to the prelate. Nevertheless, today in practice, we judge that without regard to this opinion of the doctors, the sentence of the Divine Brothers and c. unic. is observed. Here is the question: whether treasure found, or half of it according to the circumstances of the thing, in a field whose ownership is divided between the direct and the useful owner, for instance the vassal and the usufructuary, is acquired by the direct owner or the owner of the property? We judge that such treasure belongs to the direct owner, or owner of the property: l. divortio §. si fundum in fin. ff. solut. matrim. In this also the Saxon law agrees with the civil law, as Wesenbeck shows in his notes on §. Inst. de rer. div., and Heigius on §. 39 Inst. eod., fundamental constitution Electoral 53, p. 2, notwithstanding the text of the Landrecht, lib. 1, art. 35: All treasures buried in the earth deeper than a plough, belong to the royal power. For although that was formerly in use, today this text must be understood of metal veins, as the aforementioned doctors declare in the place cited, constitution 53.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Traditio est datio possessionis {a} eademque fieri potest, vel per ipsum dominum {b} vel per ejus mandatarium. {c} Requiritur tamen ad eandem ex tantis[?] persona potestas & voluntas {d} ex accipientis persona consensus & apprehenprehenfio {e} rei quæ traditur respectu ut habilis sit ad transferendum {f} & sui ipsius {g} & causæ propter quam traditur {h} ratione.
units.tr: Delivery (traditio) is the giving of possession, and it may be made either by the owner himself or by his agent. For it there is required, on the part of the person giving, power and will; on the part of the person receiving, consent and the taking hold (apprehensio) of the thing delivered. The thing must be such that it is fit to be transferred, and the delivery must also be suited to the thing itself and to the cause for which it is made.

units.la: {a} positia definitio habetur apud Cujac. lib. 11. ob. 19. & desum-ptæ ex l. 3 ff. Empt. Vend. & l. si rem tradi 28. ff. de V.O. Traditio ergo dicitur hic modus transferendi dominij quasi translatio. {b} Fieri autem potest non solum a domino, vero §. per traditionem Instit. de rer. div. l. qua ratione §. hæc quoque ff. de acqu. rer. dom. {c} Sed & ad sandatario h.e. eo qui iussu domini rem transfert §. nihil autem in terreft cum §. feq. Instit. d. l. all. text. ff. {d} Modo is qui vel cuius nomine res traditur verus dominus sit l. nemo plus potest ff. de R. J. & l. traditio 20. ff. de acqu. rer. dom. vel is qui tradit, tale quasi dominium in rem habeat, ut liberè eam administrare possit (quales tutores & curatores) quod si non habet eam alienare non potest, ut in furioso prodigo, minorenni, pupillo, marito ratione rerum dotalium immobilium aestimatarum perspicuum: velex concessione legis quasi dominus facti sit, cujusmodi creditor ratione rei oppignoratæ (e, Is verò cui res traditur in traditionem consentiat (in inventum enim nihil transferri potest) & rem traditam apprehendat, quippe quod traditio apprehensionis species sit, & mediante apprehensione perfi-citur. {f} Requiritur tamen porro ut in quem transfertur eandem accipere possit, ut res habilis ad transferendum {g} In habilis enim omnis res alienare prohibita, utpote res sacra, sancta, religiosa §. nulla Instit. de rer. div. fundus dotalis, t.t. ff. de fund. dotali & id genus res alia {b} Ut præcedat titulus seu causa habilis ad translationem dominii (utpote emptio, venditio, donatio &c.) eamq. ipsa traditio committitur & quasi sit quatuor §. venditæ verò res Instit. d. loc. nec enim nudis pactis h.e. nudis titulis l. traditionib. l. servum 27. C. de rei vind. Ieuuquam nuda ff. acqu. rer. dom. dominio rerum transferuntur. Illud non immerito quæritur an error in causa dominii translatio nem impediat? Neg. per l. cum 36. ff. de acqu. rer. dom. J. in traditionib.
units.tr: {a} This definition is found in Cujacius, Observations, book 11, ch. 19, and is taken from l. 3 ff. de Empt. Vend. and l. si rem tradi 28 ff. de V.O. Hence this mode of transferring ownership is called traditio, as if it were a translatio (transfer). {b} It may be made not only by the owner: §. per traditionem Inst. de rer. div.; l. qua ratione §. haec quoque ff. de acqu. rer. dom. {c} But also by an agent, that is, one who transfers the thing by the owner's order: §. nihil autem in terrest cum §. seq. Inst. d. l. all. text. ff. {d} Provided that the true owner is either the one to whom the thing is delivered, or the one in whose name it is delivered: l. nemo plus potest ff. de R.J.; l. traditio 20 ff. de acqu. rer. dom. Or else the one who delivers has such a quasi-ownership of the thing that he can administer it freely (as tutors and curators do). For if he does not have this, he cannot alienate it, as in the case of a madman, a prodigal, a minor, a ward, or a husband in respect of immovable dotal goods that have been valued, which is clear. Or he is quasi-owner by grant of the law, as a creditor is in respect of a pledged thing. {e} The one to whom the thing is delivered must consent to the delivery (for nothing can be transferred to one who is unaware of it), and must take hold of the thing delivered, since delivery is a kind of apprehension and is completed through apprehension. {f} It is further required that the one to whom the thing is transferred be able to receive it, so that the thing is fit to be transferred. {g} For every unfit thing is forbidden to be alienated, such as sacred, holy and religious things (§. nulla Inst. de rer. div.), a dotal fund (t.t. ff. de fund. dotali), and other things of that kind. {h} There must be a preceding title or cause fit for transferring ownership (such as sale, purchase, gift, etc.), and the delivery must be joined to it, as if it were its consequence (§. venditae vero res Inst. d. loc.). For ownership of things is not transferred by bare pacts, that is, by bare titles (l. traditionibus; l. servum 27 C. de rei vind.; nuda ff. acqu. rer. dom.). It is not unreasonably asked whether an error about the cause of ownership hinders the transfer. It does not, per l. cum 36 ff. de acqu. rer. dom.; in traditionibus.

units.la: {a} Positio definitio habetur apud Cujacium.
units.tr: The position and definition is found in Cujacius.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Traditio vel est vera vel ficta,(a)Vera dicitur quando de manu in manum res traditur (b) ficta vocatur quando ius fingit traditionem intervenisse (c).
units.tr: Traditio is either true or feigned. It is called true when the thing is handed over from hand to hand; it is called feigned when the law pretends that a delivery has taken place.

units.la: (a) Schneiddvv. & alij ita distinguunt traditionem fund. L non statim ff.de peculio (b) & prioris descriptionem habemus in S. per traditionem sub verbi tradi potest. Et à domino tradita alienantur, eaq; locum habet in solis rebus corporalibus tàm mobilibus d.§. per traditionem. tam immobilib. l.1.§.penult.ff.de acq.poss.(c) posteriòris v. delineationis varia exempla habentur §. interdum cum §.seq. [Instit.d.loc.. Eaq; in tantum porrigitur,ut per incertam voluntatem non certa personā constitutā in quam rem volumus transferre et jam fieri possit §. hoc amplius ait loc. & non solum in corporalibus rebus, sed & in incorporalibus locum habeat, cum in ijs patientia possessoris pro traditione habeatur l.2 ff.de serv. quam ad fictam traditionem sufficere exempla in all. §§. posita abundè declarant. Sufficit ergò hic fictio juris, nec reali traditione ad transferendum dominium opus est. E.g. quando rem tibi commodavi, aut locavi postea tibi eundem dono tunc non opus est, eam tibi tradam, sed sufficit patiar-rem tuam esse §.all, interdum. Sic quando tibi merces in horreo ven-do, non est opus ut ipsas merces tradam; sed traditio ficte per clavi-um dationem fieri potest §.item si quis modo venditio donatio vel alius titulus praecesserit l.clavibus ff.de contrah.empt. Citra legitimum titulum enim precedentem claves non rei tradende & transferen-de, sed custodiæ saltem causâ datæ censentur l.cum pater pluribus ff. de Leg.2. Illud hic non immeritò incidenter quæritur an de jure Saxon. in emptionib. & venditionibus ad translationem dominii traditio seu cessio judicialis requiratur; an vero qualiacunq; extrajudicialis traditio sufficiat? discrepant hic interpretes Ruchbar. p. qu. 6. n. 41. & Coler. decis. 16. n. 3. & seq. putantes cessionem sive resignationem & abdicationem Aufflassung und Werzich singularem judicialem requirere. Heigius v. p. 1. qu. 18. n. 18. existimat eam non de necessitate desiderari per gloss. ad art. 9. lib. 1. Landrecht. Heigij sententiam subscribimus.
units.tr: (a) Schneidewin and others distinguish traditio in this way: fund. L non statim ff. de peculio. (b) We have the description of the former in §. per traditionem, under the heading "sub verbi tradi potest". And things are alienated by the owner's delivery, and this applies only to corporeal things, both movable (d. §. per traditionem) and immovable (l. 1 §. penult. ff. de acq. poss.). (c) Examples of the latter, or of the outlined kind, are found in §. interdum with the following §. [Inst. d. loc.]. And this extends so far that, by an uncertain will, without a certain person being designated to whom we wish the thing to be transferred, it can already be done (§. hoc amplius, loc. cit.). It applies not only to corporeal things but also to incorporeal ones, since in these the patience of the possessor is taken as delivery (l. 2 ff. de serv.). The examples set out in the aforesaid §§. amply show that this suffices for feigned delivery. Therefore a fiction of law suffices here, and no real delivery is needed to transfer ownership. For example, when I have lent or leased a thing to you and afterwards give it to you as a gift, there is no need for me to hand it over to you; it is enough that it be allowed to remain yours (§. all. interdum). Likewise, when I sell you goods in a warehouse, there is no need for me to hand over the goods themselves; but a feigned delivery can be made by giving the keys (§. item si quis; l. clavibus ff. de contrah. empt.). Yet, without a preceding lawful title, keys are considered given not for the delivery and transfer of the thing, but at least for the purpose of custody (l. cum pater, pluribus ff. de Leg. 2). Here it is not unreasonably asked in passing whether, by the law of Saxony, a judicial delivery or cession is required for the transfer of ownership in purchases and sales, or whether any extrajudicial delivery suffices. The interpreters disagree here: Ruchbar, p. qu. 6, n. 41, and Coler, decis. 16, n. 3 et seq., think that a special judicial cession or resignation and renunciation (Auflassung und Verzicht) is required. Heigius, v. p. 1, qu. 18, n. 18, holds that it is not required of necessity, by the gloss on art. 9, lib. 1 of the Landrecht. We subscribe to Heigius's opinion.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Confusionem seu commixtionem dicimus quando duae materiae, seu corpora diversorum dominorum ita commiscentur & confunduntur, ut tamen unam novam speciem diversam unum novum corpus non constituant (a) Hoc si voluntate & consensu dominorum factum, res confusa est dividenda: (b) si vero casu, aut altero dominorum volente, altero invito factum (c) tunc similiter si quidem res confusae congerie, & ita ut separari possint, unitae, quilibet rem suam vindicare poterit (d) sin vero continuitate extremorum, & ita ut separari nequeant unitae, itidem divisio rerum sic commixtarum est instituenda (e).
units.tr: We speak of confusion or commixture when two materials, or bodies of different owners, are so mixed and fused together that they do not constitute one new species or one new different body. (a) If this is done by the will and consent of the owners, the confused thing is to be divided. (b) But if it is done by chance, or by one owner against the will of the other, then likewise: if the confused things are joined in a heap, so that they can be separated, each may claim his own thing. (c) But if they are joined by the continuity of their extremities, so that they cannot be separated, the division of the things so mixed is likewise to be carried out. (d)

units.la: (a) id enim quando unum novum corpus constituitur specificatio dicitur: quia diversa & alia species producitur & quidem si haec confusio voluntate dominorum fit, res erit dividenda, nec attendendum cuiuscunq; generis & materiae res confusae fuerint §. si duorum cum seq. Inst. de rer. div. l. 5. in pr. ff. de comm. divid. l. 7. ff. de acqu. rer. dom. Habetq; hoc casu, quia consensu & voluntate dominorum res inter se mutuae traditionis communes factae sunt §. si quod Instit. de rer. div. contra eum qui rem ita confusam solus vult retinere actio comm. divid. locum l. quidem Pomponius in sin. in pr. ff. de rei vind. Divisio tamen non pro dimidia parte secundum proportionem arithmeticam; sed pro rata ejus, quod quisquis contulit, habita ratione & quantitatis & qualitatis secundum proportionem Geome-tricam tricam est instituenda (c)Si vero vel altero ex domini invito & nolente vel casu ac fortuito commixtio facta (d)tum quod cujus fortuiti nemini imputari possint l.contractus ff.de R.J. quilibet rem suam vindicare potest, habetq; contra eum qui rem totam vult retinere actionem in rem l.3.l.f.l.23.in pr.ff.de rei vendic. quâ intentâ judex litem dirimere debet ex aequo, & ita ut quilibet tantum & tale consequatur, quantum & quale prius habuit & si hoc esse non potest, ut damno passo à commodum percipiente recompensatio fiat all §.quod si in sin. & §.2.Inst.de off.judic. modò res talis sit, ut separari possit, cujus generis plerunq; res sicca quas congerie unum per commixtionem fieri in positione diximus (e) hac enim in qualitate deficiente, reqs ejusmodi existente, ut continuitate extremorum una fiat (quod in liquidis accidit corporib.) ita ut vel difficulter vel omninò non segregari possit leg.5.in prin.ff.de rei vendic. l.adeò 7.§ sed & si 9.l.quicquid 27.ff.de acqu.rer dom. communis fit habetq; actio de comm.divid.Locum §.all.s.fi duorum Inst.non est inferenda particula NON & legendum: non idem juris ut existimat Hottom.lib.7.obs.12. Non obst.l.idem §.idem 1.ff.de rei vindic.item §.cum ex aliena Inst.de rer.div.hi enim text.loquuntur de specificatione. Non obstat etiam l.si alieni 78 ff.solut.nam cum hic per solutionem meum acceperim traditione ficta debitoris dominium in mea pecunia numerata interiit. Donell.4.(Comm.30.
units.tr: (a) For when one new body is constituted, this is called specification, because a different and new species is produced. And if this confusion is made by the will of the owners, the thing is to be divided, and it does not matter of what kind or material the confused things are (§. si duorum with the following, Inst. de rer. div.; l. 5 in pr. ff. de comm. divid.; l. 7 ff. de acqu. rer. dom.). In this case it holds, because the things have been made common to each other by the consent and will of the owners by mutual delivery (§. si quod, Inst. de rer. div.); against the one who alone wishes to keep the confused thing, the action for common division applies (l. quidem Pomponius in sin., in pr. ff. de rei vind.). The division, however, is not made into half parts by arithmetical proportion, but in proportion to what each has contributed, taking account both of quantity and of quality, by geometrical proportion. (b) But if the mixture is made by chance, or by one owner against the will and without the consent of the other, then, since it arose from an accident for which no one can be blamed (l. contractus ff. de R.J.), each may claim his own thing. He has the action in rem against the one who wishes to keep the whole thing (l. 3; l. f.; l. 23 in pr. ff. de rei vendic.), and in bringing it the judge ought to settle the dispute fairly, so that each obtains as much and of such a kind as he had before; and if this cannot be done, because of loss suffered by one and gain received by the other, compensation is made (all. §. quod si in sin. and §. 2 Inst. de off. judic.). This holds provided the thing is such that it can be separated; the kind of thing that is generally dry, which we said in the premise can be made one by mixture in a heap. For where this quality is lacking, and the thing is such that it becomes one by the continuity of its extremities (which happens with liquids), so that it cannot be separated, or only with difficulty or not at all (l. 5 in prin. ff. de rei vendic.; l. adeo 7 §. sed & si; l. 9; l. quicquid 27 ff. de acqu. rer. dom.), it becomes common, and the action for common division applies. The particle NON is not to be inserted in the text of §. all. s. fi duorum Inst., and it should not be read as Hottoman, lib. 7 obs. 12, thinks, that the law is different. Nor is it an objection that l. idem §. idem 1 ff. de rei vindic. and §. cum ex aliena Inst. de rer. div. are cited, for those texts speak of specification. Nor does l. si alieni 78 ff. solut. stand in the way, for there, since I received the money by payment, the ownership of my counted money passed through the debtor's fictitious delivery. Donellus, 4 Comm. 30.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Specificatio dicitur quando ex materia, una, vel materiis diversis nova species efficitur (a) & in hoc acquisitionis modo (b) si partim ex mea, partim ex aliena materia speciem feci novam, eandem mea manet (c) sive ò ex aliena solum modò materia speciem facio, siquidem ad priorem & rudem materiam reduci potest, ejus erit species facta cujus materia fuit (d) sin verò non reduci potest ad primam materiam ejus erit species qui operam in ea efficiendâ praestitit.(e) (a) Id enim quando unum novum corpus diversum una nova species diversa non constituitur confusio seu commixtio dicitur. (b) Gravis circa specificationem inter Sabini & Proculi Ictorum a se-ctas dissensio fuit: Sabiniani enim exististimarunt eiꝰ esse speciem qui materiae domino fuit eo quod id quod ex meo fit meum efficiatur l. d. eo §. quis ex vi[?] ff. ad exhibend. & id quod nostrum est, sive facto nostro nobis adimi haud possit l. id quod nostrum 11. ff. de R. J. Procu-liani vero putarunt, eum factae species, cum antea in nullius bonis fuerit occupanti cedat per regulam quae in §. fere Instit. de rer. div. traditur. (c) (Cujus 9(. in l. adeo §. cum quis ff. de acqu. rer. dom. & eum secutus Justinianus in §. cum ex aliena Instit. d. rer. div. hanc disce-ptationem sustulit, & constituit, ut si partim ex aliena partim ex nostra materia novam speciem faciamus, eadem nostra maneat: cum non solum operam nostram praestiterimus; sed & partem materiae dederimus. (d) Si vero ex pure & simpliciter aliena materia speciem novam facimus, ut eo casu, si ad formam priorem reduci non possit, ea juris res maneat cujus materia fuit. §. cum exaliena Instit. de rer. div. l. 7. §. cum quis l. sed sit 26. ff. de acqu. rer. dom. (e) Si vero non ita abole-ri possit forma assumpta ut pristina rursus inducatur, ut tunc effecta species specificanti cedat, eo quod tunc materia deperdita censeatur d. loc. [?] Nec obstat l. all. adeo ubi dicitur, id quod ex meo fit, meum est: e. enim tum demum locum habet, si vel egomet ipsi ipse rem feci, vel alius meo nomine, vel me mandante, vel ratificante, ut notant interpretes ad hanc l. Requiritur tamen ad id, ut specificans speciem effectam suam faciat, bona fides: nam mala fide ex aliena materia, quid efficiens, non fit eius dominus d. l. adeo §. cum quis 7. ff. de rer. dom. sed operam suam materiae, domino, donare videtur arg. l. cujus per errorem ff. de R. J. l. adeo 7. §. ex diverso 12. ff. d. t. Nec adversatur, quod Justinianus in §. cum exaliena & Cajus d. l. adeo §. cum quis non distinguant expresse inter malam & bonam fidem, eam enim distinctionem habet Paulus tacite in vocab. suo NOMINE, quam nec Justiniastinianum[?] repudiasse inde verisimile est quod Caij in d.l.adeo me-diam viam sequentis opinionem approbet & sequatur. Nec huic no-stra assertioni obstat id, quod nemo cum alterius damno locupletari debeat c.locupletari d.R.J.in 6.l.plane ʒ8.ff.de hæred.petit.l. jure na-turæ 206.ff.d.R.J. Domino enim materiæ datur actio in factum con-tra specificantem ad materiæ æstimationem consequendam. Diff. Conn.lib 3.c.6,n.3 & addit,quod etiam tum quando species plus ma-teriæ quam artis habet, licet ad pristinam formam reduci haud pos-sit,ei res factæ sit adjudicanda,cujus fuit materia, quam opinionem doctè refutat Arum.ex Instit.4.th.15.& positas distinctiones declarat Imperator multis exemplis in §.cum ex aliena Instit.de rer.div. Circa quæ tamen notandum id exemplum,quod de frumento ex spicis ex-cusso ibi ponitur, huc non quadrare.sed ex Caij institutionibus à compilatoribus Instit. Justinianarum perperàm exscriptum esse, non facto respectu ad posteriora verba Caij,quæ sunt hujus exempli correctoria,ut satis apparet ex l.7.§ cum quis 7.vers.videntur ta-men.ff.de acqu.rer.dom.ut deducit Hottom.& Anton. Matthæus ad d.§.cum ex aliena. Fornannus vult Tribonianum excusare disp.9. th.15.m.g. & adducit Imperatorum solummodo exempla in quibus quid ad priorem materiam reduci nequit,referre,nec strictè conclu-dere frumentum esse excutientis. Sed text.verba huic conciliationi reclamant. Illud hic quæritur rectè coronidis loco,an in navi idem obtineat quod in aliis speciebus & navis quoq; illius qui eam conse-cit efficiatur? Affirm. cum Baldo ad §.cum ex aliena Instit.de aeq. div.Donell.4.comm.6.n.2.Hottom.ad d.§.cum ex aliena Antonio Fa-bro6.comm. 15.per l.61.ff.de rei vindic.
units.tr: Specification is said to occur when a new species is produced from one material or from several different materials, and this is a mode of acquisition (b). If I make a new species partly from my material and partly from another's, the species remains mine (c). But if I make a species from another's material alone, then, if it can be reduced to its earlier and raw material, the species belongs to the owner of that material (d). If, however, it cannot be reduced to its first material, it belongs to the person who contributed the labour in making it (e). (a) When a new single body is produced that is not a different new species, it is called confusion or commixture. (b) There was a serious dispute about specification between the schools of the jurists Sabinus and Proculus. The Sabinians thought the species belonged to the owner of the material, since what is made from what is mine becomes mine (l. d. eo §. quis, ff. ad exhibend.), and what is ours cannot be taken from us by any act of ours (l. id quod nostrum 11, ff. de R. J.). The Proculians held that the made species, since before it was in no one's goods, belongs to the one who takes possession of it, by the rule laid down in §. fere, Inst. de rer. div. (c) (See Cujas on l. adeo §. cum quis, ff. de acqu. rer. dom.) Following him, Justinian in §. cum ex aliena, Inst. de rer. div., ended this controversy and established that if we make a new species partly from another's and partly from our own material, it remains ours, since we have contributed not only labour but also part of the material. (d) But if we make a new species from another's material purely and simply, then in that case, if it cannot be reduced to its former form, the thing remains with the owner of the material (§. cum ex aliena, Inst. de rer. div.; l. 7, §. cum quis; l. sed sit 26, ff. de acqu. rer. dom.). (e) But if the assumed form cannot be removed so that the former one is restored, then the finished species goes to the specifier, because the material is then considered lost (d. loc.). Nor does the law adeo stand in the way, where it says that what is made from mine is mine (e), for that applies only if I made the thing myself, or another made it in my name, or on my command or with my ratification, as the commentators on this law note. It is required, however, that the specifier be in good faith in order to make the species made his own. For one who makes a thing from another's material in bad faith does not become its owner (d. l. adeo §. cum quis 7, ff. de rer. dom.), but seems to give his labour as a gift to the owner (arg. l. cujus per errorem, ff. de R. J.; l. adeo 7, §. ex diverso 12, ff. d. t.). Nor does it conflict with this that Justinian in §. cum ex aliena and Gaius in d. l. adeo §. cum quis do not expressly distinguish between bad and good faith. Paul makes that distinction tacitly in his word NOMINE, and it is probable that Justinian did not reject it, since Gaius in that law approves and follows the middle opinion. Nor does what is said here stand against this assertion, namely that no one ought to be enriched at another's loss (c. locupletari, d. R. J. in 6; l. plane 38, ff. de hæred. petit.; l. jure naturæ 206, ff. d. R. J.). For the owner of the material is given an action in factum against the specifier to recover the value of the material. Connanus (Diff., lib. 3, c. 6, n. 3) adds that even when the species contains more material than labour, and cannot be reduced to its former form, the made thing should nonetheless be adjudged to the owner of the material. Arnoldus learnedly refutes this opinion (ex Instit. 4, th. 15), and the Emperor declares the distinctions laid down with many examples in §. cum ex aliena, Inst. de rer. div. Here, however, it must be noted that the example there given of grain threshed from the ears does not fit this rule. It was copied wrongly by the compilers of Justinian's Institutes from the Institutes of Gaius, without regard to the later words of Gaius that correct this example, as is sufficiently clear from l. 7, §. cum quis 7, vers. videntur tamen, ff. de acqu. rer. dom., as Hottoman and Antonius Matthaeus deduce on d. §. cum ex aliena. Fornanus wishes to excuse Tribonian (disp. 9, th. 15, m. g.) and maintains that the Emperors' examples refer only to cases where a thing cannot be reduced to its earlier material, and do not strictly conclude that the grain belongs to the one who threshed it. But the words of the text oppose this reconciliation. Here, as a corollary, the question is rightly raised whether the same holds for a ship as for other species, so that the ship too becomes the property of the one who built it. The answer is affirmative, with Baldus on §. cum ex aliena, Inst. de aeq. div.; Donellus 4, comm. 6, n. 2; Hottoman on the same §. cum ex aliena; Antonius Faber, 6 comm. 15, on l. 61, ff. de rei vindic.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Accessioni naturali nobis acquiruntur ea, quæ ipsâ natura operante rebus nostris accedunt, vel ex rebus no-stris proficiscuntur (a) Et hujusmodi accessionis species, præcipuæ, ad quas aliæ referri possunt, [?]ex sunt scilicet alluvio{b} insula in flumine nata partus ancillarum{f} fructus sponte provenientes fundi{g} vel nostri aut quoad pleuum{h} aut quoad utile{i} dominium vel alieni bona fide à nobis possessi{k}.
units.tr: By natural accession we acquire those things which come to our things by nature working alone, or which proceed from our things (a). The principal species of this accession, to which the others can be referred, are: alluvion, an island born in a river, the offspring of female slaves, fruits that grow spontaneously, the ownership of our field, whether full or usufructuary, or of another's goods possessed by us in good faith.

units.la: {a} Vidimus hactenus accessionis latissimè sumptæ species duas priores jam consequens est, ut proprie dictam accessionem videamus, quæ id quod rei accedit nostra vel ex nostra re proficiscitur, nostrum efficitur juxta vulgatam regulam: accessorium sequitur naturam sui principalis l.cum principalis 178.ff.d.R.I.c.accessorium de R.I. l.in 6. Harum una quidem principalis rectè naturalis vocatur, ideò quod maximè naturâ operante perficiatur. fund.§.insula cum trib. f.q.&§.fi qs cum duo.feqq.§§.Inftit.de rer.div.(b) huius prima species alluvio (quæ nihil aliud quam incrementum latens) eam terræ portionem, quæ à flumine latenter & sensim nostro fundo adjicitur nobis acquirit §.præterea Inftit.d.rer.div.l.adeò 7. §. 1. l. in agris 16.ff de acqu.rer.dom.l.1.C.de alluv.modo agri quibus portio adjicitur sint arcifinei seu occupatorij d.l.16.l.1.§.6.ff.de fluminib. qui quales declarat Con.in.lib.3.c.s n.4.& seq.in limitatis enim h.e.certis limitibus distinctis agris jus alluvionis locum non habet d.l.16.ff.d.acqu.rer.dom.Diff.Conn.3.comm.s.n.4.vid.Donell.4.comm.26.& 27 c.& Baptistam Emium lib 1.d.alluv.c.17. Illud hic non immeritò quæritur an ad usfufructuarium, Emphyteutam & vafallum jus alluvionis quoq; pertineat? Affirm.defendemus per l.item 9. huic ff.de Ufufr.l.fi fundus 16 in pr.ff.de pignorib.& ea quæ habet Schraderus d.feud.p.r.c.6.n.26.& Heig p 2.q.ult.Ea v.terræ portio, quæ reperenti no motu,& ita ut animadverti possit, non paulatim & latenter fundo nostro adijcitur non efficitur nostra, sed à suo domino antequam coaluat, quo vis tempore vindicare potest §.quod si vis Inft.d.lo.l.adeò §.1.ff.de acqu.rer.dom.Sit tamen tam diu negligentia suâ à domino non vindicatur donec coaluat, per hanc consolidationem, & quasi fundo nostro agglutinationem nostra efficitur all §,& all.l.adeò l.9 §.
units.tr: {a} We have so far seen the two earlier species of accession, taken in the broadest sense. It follows that we should now look at accession properly so called, by which what comes to a thing, or proceeds from our thing, becomes ours, according to the common rule that the accessory follows the nature of its principal (l. cum principalis 178, ff. d. R. I.; c. accessorium, de R. I., in 6). Of these, one is rightly called natural, because it is accomplished chiefly by nature working alone (fund. §. insula cum trib.; f. q. & §. fi qs cum duo, and following, Inst. de rer. div.). (b) The first species of this is alluvion, which is nothing other than a hidden increase. It gives us acquisition of that portion of land which the river adds to our field secretly and gradually (§. præterea, Inst. d. rer. div.; l. adeo 7, §. 1; l. in agris 16, ff. de acqu. rer. dom.; l. 1, C. de alluv.). The fields to which the portion is added must be arcifinious or occupatory (d. l. 16; l. 1, §. 6, ff. de fluminib.). Connanus (lib. 3, c. 5, n. 4 and following) explains what sort these are. For where the fields are limited, that is, distinguished by fixed boundaries, the right of alluvion does not apply (d. l. 16, ff. d. acqu. rer. dom.; Diff. Conn. 3, comm. 5, n. 4; see Donellus 4, comm. 26 and 27, and Baptista Emius, lib. 1, d. alluv., c. 17). Here it is not unreasonably asked whether the right of alluvion also belongs to the usufructuary, the emphyteuta and the vassal. We shall defend the affirmative by l. item 9, huic ff. de usufr.; l. si fundus 16 in pr., ff. de pignorib.; and by what Schraderus has (d. feud. p. r. c. 6, n. 26) and Heig (p. 2, q. ult.). That portion of land, however, which is added to our field not gradually and secretly, but by a movement that can be observed, does not become ours, but remains with its owner before it coalesces; he may claim it at any time (§. quod si, Inst. d. loc.; l. adeo §. 1, ff. de acqu. rer. dom.). Yet if the owner, through his own negligence, does not claim it until it coalesces, then by this consolidation, and as it were agglutination to our field, it becomes ours (all. §.; all. l. adeo; l. 9 §.

units.la: Alfenus 2.ff.de damno infect. quod & in arboribus obtinet, quae ad fundum nostrum vi fluminis adiecta antequam radices egerint, a suo domino vindicari possunt: postquam vero radices egerunt, nostra efficiuntur d.l.9.§.Alfenus 2.ff.de dam.infect.l.ied fi 26.§. 2.ff. de acqu.rer.dom. Idem Pomponius §. f.ff.d.rei vindic.(c) Insulam h.e. terram in solo seu mari (inde enim nomen habet, quod maxime in mari sita sit) quod attinet hac in mari nata (vobis enim de insulis quae semper fuerunt cuius generis Corsica, Creta & similes sic mo non est) similiter ut mare nullius est in bonis arg. §. & quidem lusture de rer. div. & proinde occupanti cedit §.Insul. Insulit.d.loc.adeo 7.§.3.ff. de acq rer.dom. Qui aqui animo eo eam ingreditur ut eandem occupet, nec hoc casu necesse est singulas terrae glebas apprehendi l.4.ff.de acqu.rer.dom. Iurisdictionem tamen in insula sic occupata is retinet cuius est provincia arg. l. insulae 9.ff.de judic. Vult ad §. Insula 22. Insulit. d. rer. div. Nam vero in fluminis medio eorum est communis quorum fundi flumen attingunt modo fundi artificium non limitati sint l.1. §.insula ff.de flum. §.insula 22. Insulit de rer div. eo quod alveus quatenus non tegitur fluminis privatus sit, & ad proximè accolentium dominium pertineat l.ergo 30.§.1.& 2.ff. d.acqu.rer.dom. Cuius tamen proportione quae ipsius fundi flumen attingit all. §. insula all. l. adeo §. insula & l. inter eos ff. de acqu. rer, dom. acquiritur. Cum quo convenit Jus Saxon. art.56.lib.2. Landr. Et denique proprior est quam fluminis medietati, eorum quorum fundi proximius adjacent all.textib. Et haec acquisitio insulae de qua hic loquimur intelligenda est, tam te proprietate, tam de usu l. adeo §.3. inter 29.ff.de acq.rer.dom. Don.4.Com.11. Dis. Cuj. 14.obs.11 per l.pen. §. ult.ff.de acq.rer.dom. Resp.vid.apud Pac.Cod. Sinv. qu.93. Sin flumen sinuose trascurrere incipit, ita ut superius dividatur, & inferiori rursus uniatur ac ita ex agro alicuius insulam efficit, ea insula sic effecta ejus manet, cujus ager antea fuit §. insula & §. all. adeo §. quod fit d. art.56. Landrecht. Similiter requiritur Insula flumius alveo jam firmiter aggluagglutinata ut sit. Si enim nondum alveus aret; sed solummodo virgultis aliâq; materiâ in ipso flumine fuslinetur[?] publica est, nec ad privatorum dominia pertinet, eo quod flumina in se publici juris sint l. penult. C. quæ res. de acqu. rer. dom. (d) Vt autem insula sic & alveus derelictus h.e. fossa per quam flumen dilabitur seu venter fluminis, eorum efficitur, qui prope ripam prædia arcifinia & occupatoria h.e. prædia non limitata possident. Et hoc casu pro quantitate prædij, quantitas alvei derelicti cuius aestimanda §. quod finaturali Instit. d. rer. div. l.1 §.1. ff. de fluminib. l. adeo 7 §.1 ergo §.1. ff. d. acqu. rer. dom. Licet quam diu alveus flumini inservit juris publici sit, in tantum ut & ager privatus non modo per alveum fluminis publicus fiat, non quidem proprietate, sed usu l. adeo 7 §.5 eo quod flumen publicum sit non quod ad proprietatem, sed quo ad usum, ut deducit Vult. in tit. Instit. 2. rer. div. n. 24. in pr. ex l.1. in pr. ff. d. interdict. & l. fluminum ff. d. damn. infect. Sed & flumine alveum longo intervallo post delinquente, non prioris domini rursus efficiatur, sed iis qui prædia prope ripam possident, cedit ut all. §. quod si naturali & all. l. adeo. Diversa tamen ratio est in inundato agro: Secedente enim aquâ, ager in iis rursus cedit quorum anteà fuit §. alia sane Instit. d. loc. l. 30. §. alluvio ff. de acq. rer. dom. Cui num obst. l. Attius 38. ff. eod. loquitur enim de mutatione alvei l. 23. l. 24. ff. quib. modis usufr. amitt. quod & tum obtinet, si alveus a flumine noviter factus, repente exsiccetur, & a flumine deflituatur l. adeo 7. §. quod si & §. aliud sane l. ergo §. alluvio ff. de acqu. rer. dom. Donell. 4. Comm. c. 28. Baptista Æmilius d. jure alluvionis §.1. n. 2. & seq. c. 13. Diff. Conn. 2. comm. §. contrariorum argum. dissolutionem vid. apud Pac. cent. 2. quæst. 88. (e)
units.tr: Alfenus, 2 ff. de damno infecto, which also holds for trees carried onto our land by the force of a river before they have taken root: these can still be claimed by their former owner, but once they have taken root they become ours. d.l.9 §. Alfenus 2 ff. de dam. infect.; l. ied fi 26 §. 2 ff. de acqu. rer. dom. The same Pomponius, §. f. ff. d. rei vindic. (c) An island, that is, land in the soil or in the sea (for it has its name from lying mostly in the sea). As to what arises in this sea (for we are not speaking here of islands that have always existed, such as Corsica, Crete and the like), it is, like the sea, among things belonging to no one, arg. §. & quidem lusture de rer. div., and so it falls to whoever occupies it, §. Insul. Insulit. d. loc. adeo 7 §. 3 ff. de acq. rer. dom. Whoever enters it with the intention of occupying it does not, in this case, have to take hold of each clod of earth, l.4 ff. de acqu. rer. dom. Jurisdiction over an island so occupied, however, is retained by the one whose province it is, arg. l. insulae 9 ff. de judic. Vultejus on §. Insula 22, Insulit. d. rer. div. For in the middle of a river, the bed belongs in common to those whose estates the river touches, provided the estates are not bounded by a surveyed line, l.1 §. insula ff. de flum.; §. insula 22, Insulit. de rer. div., because the bed, so far as it is not covered by the river, is private and belongs to the ownership of those living nearest to it, l. ergo 30 §. 1 & 2 ff. d. acqu. rer. dom. In proportion to the part of the river that touches each estate, it is acquired (all. §. insula, all. l. adeo, §. insula, & l. inter eos ff. de acqu. rer. dom.). The Saxon law agrees with this, art. 56, lib. 2, Landr. And finally, the island is nearer to the half of the river belonging to those whose estates lie closest to it, all. textib. This acquisition of the island of which we speak here is to be understood as applying both to ownership and to use, l. adeo §. 3, inter 29 ff. de acq. rer. dom.; Don. 4 Com. 11 Dis.; Cuj. 14 obs. 11; per l. pen. §. ult. ff. de acq. rer. dom.; Resp. see Pac. Cod., Sinv. qu. 93. But if the river begins to wind sinuously, so that it divides above and rejoins below, and in this way makes an island out of someone's field, that island, so formed, remains the property of the one whose field it was before, §. insula & §. all. adeo, §. quod fit, d. art. 56, Landrecht. Likewise, an island is required to be firmly joined to the bed of the river. For if the bed is not yet dry, but the river merely supports brushwood and other material, it is public and does not belong to private ownership, since rivers are themselves of public right, l. penult. C. quae res de acqu. rer. dom. (d) But just as with an island, so too an abandoned bed, that is, the ditch through which the river flows, or the channel of the river, becomes the property of those who hold estates beside the bank that are unbounded, that is, not surveyed, and open to occupation. In this case the quantity of the abandoned bed is to be assessed according to the quantity of the estate, §. quod si naturali Instit. d. rer. div.; l.1 §.1 ff. de fluminib.; l. adeo 7 §.1 ergo §.1 ff. d. acqu. rer. dom. Although, so long as the bed serves the river, it is of public right, to such an extent that even a private field becomes public through the river's bed, not indeed in ownership but in use, l. adeo 7 §.5, because the river is public not as to ownership but as to use, as Vultejus deduces, in tit. Instit. 2 rer. div. n. 24, in pr., from l.1 in pr. ff. d. interdict. and l. fluminum ff. d. damn. infect. But if the river afterwards leaves its bed for a long interval, the bed does not return to its former owner, but passes to those who hold estates near the bank, as in all. §. quod si naturali and all. l. adeo. The reasoning is different, however, in the case of a flooded field: when the water recedes, the field returns to those to whom it belonged before, §. alia sane Instit. d. loc.; l. 30 §. alluvio ff. de acq. rer. dom. Nor does l. Attius 38 ff. eod. stand against this, for it speaks of a change of bed, l. 23, l. 24 ff. quib. modis usufr. amitt. This also holds when a newly made bed is suddenly dried up and abandoned by the river, l. adeo 7 §. quod si & §. aliud sane, l. ergo §. alluvio ff. de acqu. rer. dom.; Donell. 4 Comm. c. 28; Baptista Aemilius, d. jure alluvionis §.1 n. 2 & seq., c. 13 Diff.; Conn. 2 comm. §. contrariorum argum. For the solution see Pac. cent. 2, quaest. 88. (e)

units.la: Quarto fœtus ex animalibus nostris proveniens non solum ijs quorum plenum, sed & ijs quorum utile saltem habemus dominium, nobis cedit §. item ea Instit. d. loc. l. 6. ff. de acqu. rer. dom. & l. 5. §. 2. ff. de rei vind. ubi JCtanquit: Si equam tuam equus meus prægnantem fecerit, eo esse tuum, sed meum quod natum est, quod ipsum ex usufructuario manifestum est, cui cedit licet utile saltem dominium habeat §. in pecudum Instit. d. l. (l) partus ancillarum quoq; similiter nobis cedit eo quod partus ventrem per l. f. §. 2. ff. de rei vind. & arg. l. naturae 24. ff. de stat. hom. & consequenter ventris domini [?] §. 2. sequitur, nisi quod in hoc illud peculiare sit, quod usufructu- arii [?] leg. [?] aliter essencefso, non usufr. ucturio, sed proprietario domino acquiratur, eo quod homo ob suam excellentiam non sit in fructu alie. §. pecudum & l. 68. ff. de usufruct. Obstare videtur l. 10. l. Falcidia 24. ff. ad L. Falcid. & l. Paulus respondit 4. ff. d. usuris. Respondit apud Forman. disputat. p. th 12. & Graf. §. mliscell. c. 8. (g) De nig. fructus fundi quod attinet hi sunt aut naturales aut industriales l. fructus in pecudum l. qui si §. in alieno ff. d. usfur. & ex his naturales & sponte provenientes (de his enim hic in fructificatione nobis solummodo sermo est) ut foli accessorium possessori cedunt certa tamen cum distinctione. (h) Si enim fundus totaliter pleni dominii juris, noster est totaliter & individualiter efficiuntur nostri arg. §. all item ea. Idq; ea ex ratione, quod nihil tam naturale sit, quam id quod ex re nostra provenit, nostrum fiat. (i) Si vero saltem quae ad usumfructum, vel colonorum jure, aliove utili dominii titulo nostrum est, ista jure per mortem usufructuarij vel coloni finito, percepti, h. e. a solo separati & in horreum recondituq; nostri facti esse efficiuntur, pendentes & superstites in horreum non dum recondit non similiter, sed eidem proprietario domino cedunt leg. si fructuarius messem leg. si apes 26. l. servus 61. §. locavi ff. d. furt. §. is vero Instit. d. rer. divis. in quo vocabulum fere non exterminandum putamus per l. 14. §. ult. ff. Locati leg. viam to C. de locat. Idq; propterea, quod fructus pendentes pars soli esse censentur l. fructus ff. d. rei vindic. morte autem usufructuarii, jus quod in solo fundi istius habuit ut personale extinguitur §. sin. Instit. d. usufr. Diss. Cujac. in notis Instit. post. & putat deberi heredi fructuarii fructus pro rata temporis, quo constituit usufructus per l. §. §. 4. ff. si usufructus pet. & l. 32. & penult. ff. de usufruct. legat. quam opinionem Cujac. refutat. Hartm. lib. 1. quaest. 24. n. 17. (k) Quod si fundum alienum ut nostrum bona fide h. e. non aliter quam ut nostrum sit, scientes & exstillimantes possidemus, quam diu in bona fide fumus omnes in provenientes fructus naturales l. bonæ fidei 48. l. qui scit § 1. l. in pecudum. 28. ff. d. usur. § si quis Instit. de rer. div. nostros efficimus. Quod si alter verus dominus nondum fundo præscripto (si enim præscriptus esset, vindicatio non habet locum) eum vindicat, nosq; ita male fidei possessores esse incipimus, tunc dominus fundi suos facit naturales fructus pendentes, ex eo quod pars fundi esse censeantur l. fructus 44. ff. de rei vindic. & omnes tam extantes tam consumptos, qui post malam fidem supervenientem, vel percepti sunt, vel percipi potuerunt l. in sin. C. de petit. hæred. l. certum 22. C. d. rei vind. Ut eis[?] bonæ fidei possessor non habet titulum suæ possessionis, h.e. quando quidem illum suum fundum esse certò statuit, quo titulo autem an ex emptione, an donatione, ipse vel sui antecessores eundem acceperint, ignorat, ante malam fidem perceptos h.e. quoquo modo solo remotos, licet in horreum non dum reconditi fuerint l. 13. ff. quib. mod. usufr. amitt. l. bonæ fidei ff. de acqu. rer. dom. l. qui scit § 1. ff. d. Usur. tam consumptos ex quibus bonæ fidei possessor fructus [?] quibus bona fiunt possessor fac. ut est locupletior Didac.Covar.r.resol.c.3.per l.sed si §.consuluit ff.d.hæred petit.ex quo ex quo text interpretationem l.Nesennius §. fundum ff.d. re judic.de- fumendam, putamus cum Foman. disp. Inst.tit. 21. lit. c. Diff.Fach.1 contr.58 ita ut eorum æstimationem bonae fidei possessor præstare te- neatur,l.si me & Titium ff si certum petat per § fundum l.Nesennius ff.d re judic l r.& meff.d reb.credit.l.idem ff.de condict.indeb. quam extantes l. fructus & fundi d l bonae fidei d.l.qui scit l.in pecudum ff. d.Usur. Bonae fidei vero possessor, hoc casu solos fructus perceptos h. e.agro remotos, licet in horreum nondum reconditi fuerint arg mod. adduct L.L. Siquidem suae possessionis titulum habet h.c. fi scit quo jure ipse & antecessores sui hunc fundum possideant, omnes tam extantes, quam consumptos §.si qui Instit.d.rer.div.l.bonae fidei ff.d. acqu.rer.dom. Sin v. titulu non habet, solos consumptos ex quibus non factus est locupletior arg.all.l.l,sed si §.consuluit ff.de haered.petit. capi. suos facit. Male fidei possessorem quod attinet, is e fructibus naturalibus, nec perceptos sive extent, sive consumpti sint, nec percipiendos suos uos facit, sed omnes sive indè locupletior factus sit sive non fundi domino restituere tenetur, l.si navis §.in l.1 uctus ff.d.rei vind.& § all. si quis & l.25.infin ff.d.usur. Et ejusmodi fructus à mala fide possessore repeti possunt si quidem extant rei vindicatione: sin v. consumpti condict. sine causa l.malâ fide C. de Condict.ex lege.
units.tr: Fourthly, offspring born from our animals belong to us, not only when we have full ownership of the mother but also when we have only useful ownership. This is stated in §. item ea of the Institutes, in the same title, in l. 6 ff. de acquirendo rerum dominio, and in l. 5 §. 2 ff. de rei vindicatione, where the jurist says: "If my stallion has made your mare pregnant, the foal is yours, but what is born is mine." This is plain also in the case of a usufructuary, to whom the offspring falls although he has only useful ownership, §. in pecudum of the Institutes, cited above. Likewise the offspring of female slaves falls to us, because the offspring follows the womb, l. f. §. 2 ff. de rei vindicatione; and by argument from l. naturae 24 ff. de statu hominum, and consequently it follows for the owner of the womb, §. 2. The one peculiarity is that, where the mother belongs to a usufructuary, the offspring is acquired not by the usufructuary but by the owner of the property, because a human being, on account of his excellence, is not counted among the fruits of another's property: §. pecudum, and l. 68 ff. de usufructu. l. 10, l. Falcidia 24 ff. ad legem Falcidiam, and l. Paulus respondit 4 ff. de usuris seem to stand in the way, and the answer is given by Formanus, disputation p. th. 12, and Graevius, §. miscellanea c. 8. As for the natural fruits of a field, these are either natural or industrial, l. fructus, in pecudum, l. qui si, §. in alieno ff. de usufructu; and of these the natural ones which come forth spontaneously (for it is of these alone that we are speaking here, in the matter of fruit-bearing) fall to the possessor as an accessory of the soil, though with a certain distinction. (h) For if we have full ownership of the field, the fruits become wholly and individually ours, by argument from §. all item ea; and this for the reason that nothing is so natural as that what comes from our property should become ours. (i) But if we hold only the usufruct, or hold by the right of a tenant, or by some other title of useful ownership, then the fruits, once the usufructuary or tenant has died and his right has ended, if they have been gathered, that is separated from the soil and stored in the barn, become ours; but those still hanging and not yet stored in the barn do not fall in the same way, but belong to the owner of the property: l. si fructuarius, messem; l. si apes 26; l. servus 61, §. locavi ff. de furtis; §. is vero of the Institutes de rerum divisione, in which word we think it should not be dismissed as worthless, per l. 14, §. ult. ff. locati, and the law "viam to C. de locato". This is because pending fruits are considered part of the soil, l. fructus ff. de rei vindicatione; but on the death of the usufructuary, the right that he had in the soil of that field is extinguished as personal, §. sin. of the Institutes de usufructu. Cujacius, in the notes on the later Institutes, holds that the heir of the usufructuary is owed fruits in proportion to the time for which the usufruct was constituted, per l. §. 4 ff. si usufructus petatur, and l. 32 and penult. ff. de usufructu legato; an opinion which Cujacius refutes. Hartmann, lib. 1, quaest. 24, n. 17. (k) But if we possess another's field in good faith, that is, as though it were our own, believing and supposing it to be ours, then for as long as we are in good faith we make all the natural fruits that arise ours: l. bonae fidei 48; l. qui scit §. 1; l. in pecudum 28 ff. de usuris; §. si quis of the Institutes de rerum divisione. But if the true owner, before the field has been prescribed (for if it had been prescribed, the action of vindication would not lie), claims it, and we thus begin to be possessors in bad faith, then the owner of the field makes his own the pending natural fruits, because they are regarded as part of the field, l. fructus 44 ff. de rei vindicatione; and all fruits, whether still extant or consumed, which were either gathered or could have been gathered after the bad faith supervened, l. in fine C. de petitione hereditatis; l. certum 22 C. de rei vindicatione. A possessor in good faith, who has no title to his possession (that is, while indeed he holds firmly that the field is his, but does not know by what title, whether by purchase or gift, he or his predecessors acquired it), makes his own the fruits gathered before the bad faith, that is, those removed from the soil in any way, even if they have not yet been stored in the barn: l. 13 ff. quibus modis usufructus amittitur; l. bonae fidei ff. de acquirendo rerum dominio; l. qui scit §. 1 ff. de usuris; and also those consumed, from which the possessor in good faith has not been made richer, Didacus Covarruvias, resol. c. 3, per l. sed si §. consuluit ff. de hereditatis petitione, ex quo text. This interpretation of the law Nerva-type text, we think, is to be adopted with Formanus, disp., Institutes tit. 21, lit. c, and Fachinetus, 1 contr. 58, so that the possessor in good faith is bound to make good their value: l. si me et Titium ff. si certum petatur; per §. fundum; l. Nesennius ff. de rei iudicata; l. 1 and l. mef. de rebus creditis; l. idem ff. de condictione indebiti. [The extant fruits: l. fructus and fundi, d. l.; l. bonae fidei, d. l. qui scit; l. in pecudum ff. de usuris.] But the possessor in good faith, in this case, only the fruits gathered, that is removed from the field, even if they were not yet stored in the barn, by argument from the same authorities. Since he has a title to his possession, that is, if he knows by what right he and his predecessors hold this field, he makes his own all fruits, both those still extant and those consumed, §. si qui of the Institutes de rerum divisione; l. bonae fidei ff. de acquirendo rerum dominio. But if he has no title, he makes his own only the consumed fruits from which he was not made richer, by argument from the same l. sed si §. consuluit ff. de hereditatis petitione, chapter. A possessor in bad faith, as far as natural fruits are concerned, is bound to restore to the owner of the field all those fruits, whether gathered or not, whether still extant or consumed, and whether or not he has been made richer thereby, l. si navis §. in l. fructus ff. de rei vindicatione; and §. all. si quis; and l. 25 in fine ff. de usuris. Fruits of this kind can be demanded from a possessor in bad faith by the action of vindication if they still exist; but if they have been consumed, by the condiction without cause, l. malâ fide C. de condictione ex lege.

units.la: Accessione industriali nobis acquiruntur ea, quæ non naturâ; sed industria & labore humano è rebus nostris proveniunt {a} quod ipsum fit, vel rem rei, vel rem solo conjungendo. {b} Hoc contingit aut plantatione & satione {c} aut in ædificatione {d} illud aut intextione {e} aut pictura {f} aut scriptura {g}.
units.tr: By industrial accession are acquired to us those things which come forth from our property not by nature but by industry and human labour. This happens either by joining thing to thing or thing to soil. It takes place either by planting and sowing, or in building, or in weaving, or in painting, or in writing.

units.la: {a} arg.§.si tamen alienam & § cum in suo solo cum §§.s. seqq. Inst.d.rer.div.
units.tr: (a) By argument from §. si tamen alienam, and §. cum in suo solo, with §§. seqq. of the Institutes de rerum divisione.

units.la: {b} ita distinguit elegantissimè Foman.disp. 9. th. 16. & 24. Et quidem in ea accessione, quâres solo conjungitur, hæc unica observatur regula: quod res semper solo cedat. In eâ verò accessione quâres rei conjungitur distinguendum an res quæ rei conjungitur illius rei cui conjungitur pars formalis fiat, annon? Priori casu ei cedit rei, quæ novæ formæ introducendæ causa fuit principalis: Posteriori casu res conjuncta simpliciter ei rei cedit, cui conjungitur, ut elegantissimè decidit Gædd. ad l.Labeo 14.n.11.ff.d.V.S. & eum secutus Foman. d.disp.9.th.24.& 25.
units.tr: (b) Formanus distinguishes this very elegantly, disp. 9, th. 16 and 24. In that accession in which a thing is joined to the soil, only this one rule is observed: that the thing always yields to the soil. In that accession in which one thing is joined to another thing, one must distinguish whether the thing joined to the other becomes a formal part of the thing to which it is joined or not. In the former case it yields to that thing which was the principal cause of introducing the new form; in the latter case the joined thing simply yields to that thing to which it is joined, as Gaddeus elegantly decides on l. Labeo 14, n. 11 ff. de verborum significatione, and Formanus, following him, d. disp. 9, th. 24 and 25.

units.la: {c} Plantata §.si Titulus l.adeò § ult. ff. d.acqu.rer.dom.l.1.& 7.ff.d.rei vind. Satâ §.qua ratione Inst.d rer. div. l.qui scit 25.ff.de Usur.l.19.in pr.ff.d.acqu.rer.dom. solo cedunt, & proindè si nos alienam plantam in nostrum fundum ponimus, alienumque semen nostro fundo inserimus, vel si alter quispiam plantam, suum semen, nostro fundo inserit, sic implantata, insita, nobis acquiruntur modò radices egerint; antequam enim radices egerint à suo domino vindicari possunt: radices enim sunt quasi gluten, quo planta vel arbor solo agglutinatur.
units.tr: Planted things (§ si Titius; l. adeò § ult. ff. de acquir. rer. dom.; l. 1 & 7 ff. de rei vindic.) and sown things (§ qua ratione Inst. de rer. div.; l. qui scit 25 ff. de usur.; l. 19 in pr. ff. de acquir. rer. dom.) pass with the soil. Therefore, if we place another's plant in our field, or insert another's seed into our field, or if someone else inserts his own plant or seed into our field, then the things so planted or grafted become ours, provided they have put down roots. For before they have put down roots they can still be claimed by their owner, since roots are as it were the glue by which a plant or tree is fastened to the soil.

units.la: Si ergo in nostro fundo arbor alterius à nobis bonâ fide insita fuerit, dominum priorem amittit, & mostra efficitur l.adeo 7.§.ult.ff.d.acq rer.dom.l.1.&3.ff.de rei vindic. in tantum ut rursus erutus ad priorem dominum non revertatur l. sed si §.arbor.ff.d.acqu.rer.dom. Nec obstat l.idem §d.arbore ff.d.rei vindic. Ille enim text priori domino utilem solummodo tribuit actionem, non directam, & sic eum non constituit dominum, ut respondet Delrio ad d.l.idem. Unde & si vicini arbor in confinio posita in meo fundo ita radices egit ut a terra mea alatur, mea efficitur, adeo ut fructus ejusdem inter nos sint dividendi, modo ab initio ubi coepit vitalis esse utriusq; fundi terram praefferit §.si Titius Instit.de rer.div. d.l.adeo: Ea enim arbor quae non est posita in fine licet in utroq; fundo radices egerit communis non est l.6 in sin.ff.arbor.furt.caesar. Sed ego fructus inde in alienum decidentes fundum, etiam demum post tertium diem colligere possum l.unic ff.d.gland.legend.
units.tr: If, therefore, a tree belonging to another is grafted in good faith by us into our field, it loses its former owner and is made ours (l. adeo 7 § ult. ff. de acquir. rer. dom.; l. 1 & 3 ff. de rei vindic.), to such an extent that, once uprooted, it does not return to its former owner (l. sed si § arbor ff. de acquir. rer. dom.). Nor does l. idem § de arbore ff. de rei vindic. stand in the way. For that text gives the former owner only a useful action, not a direct one, and so does not make him owner, as Del Rio answers on that same law. Hence also, if a neighbour's tree standing on the boundary has put down roots so that it is nourished from my soil, it becomes mine, so that its fruit must be divided between us, provided that from the beginning, when it began to live, it was rooted in the soil of both fields (§ si Titius Inst. de rer. div.; d. l. adeo). For a tree that is not planted on the boundary is not held in common, even if it has put down roots in both fields (l. 6 in fin. ff. arbor. furt. caesa). But the fruit that falls from it into my field I may gather even after the third day (l. unic. ff. de glandibus legendis).

Ius Sax. hæc omnia duob. axiom.atibus determinat, quorum primum ita se habet[?]: colens fundum alienum bonâ fide lucratur fructus, malâ fide, & fructus & operam perdit gl. Landrecht lib.2.art.46.[?]
units.tr: Saxon law, however, provides that fruit falling from such a tree that is not held in common belongs not to the tree but to the owner of the field onto which it falls (l. 2 art. 52, Landrecht; Weichbild art. 157). Indeed, the fruit that someone picks from the branches of a neighbouring tree hanging over his own field may be taken by him, and the owner of the field over which the branches hang is adjudged to have it (d. art., Landrecht, where the text says: "If the hop-vine winds itself around a tree, whoever has the root in his yard may take the hops; what follows it is his, but what does not follow remains the neighbour's."). And, what is more, Saxon law allows the owner of the field next to the tree to cut off the branches hanging near his boundary (Weichbild art. 126 & 127). In these cases, however, the person who sowed or planted is given an exception of fraud, if we or he himself, in good faith, that is, not knowing the field to be another's, have sown in the field, or have planted something in it, and he wishes to keep the thing sown or planted against the owner's will, unless he pays the expenses and the value of the seed or plant (l. 48 ff. de rei vindic.). For although fruits are gathered not by right of the seed but by right of the soil (l. qua ratione 9 ff. de acquir. rer. dom.; d. l. qui scit), the owner of the field is nevertheless bound to restore the expenses (l. plane 38 ff. de petit. haered.) or to hand over the fruits (l. 14 ff. de condict. indeb.). By Saxon law the sower does not recover his expenses (Landrecht lib. 2 art. 46). If, however, we have sown or planted another's thing in our field in bad faith, four actions lie against us for the owner of the thing: namely, the action for production, the action for recovery of the thing, the action for condiction, and the action of theft (argument from the words: "just as he who has built on another's soil", § all. qua ratione, as Schneidewin has shown on § in suo solo Inst. de rer. div. n. 6). On the other hand, if someone in bad faith, that is, knowing that the field is not his own, inserts or plants something in his field, he loses the thing inserted or planted (argument from l. cujus per errorem ff. de R.J.). And what we have so far said about sowing and planting holds not only for the field that belongs to us with full ownership, but also for a usufructuary, and for a field which, though another's, we possess in good faith as our own. For as regards a field belonging to us by full ownership, natural as well as industrial fruits of things planted or sown in our field, whether by our own labour or by another's, become ours, according to that rule: "nothing is so natural as that what comes from our property should become ours." The same law holds for a usufructuary field: the usufructuary makes his own, as natural fruits, so also all fruits (whether from his own thing or from another's thing planted or sown by labour, things sown or planted belong to the soil), with the distinction however which we have set out above concerning natural fruits, by the general words of § is v. Inst. de rer. div. Similarly, one who possesses in good faith another's field as his own, not yet prescribed, makes his own, when the owner interrupts the prescription, not only natural fruits (according to the distinction laid down above) but also industrial fruits from his own or another's labour, planted or sown, by the rule (sown and planted things belong to the soil), both consumed and surviving, whether he possesses with or without title (§ si quis Inst. de rer. div.; l. 48 ff. de acquir. rer. dom.; l. 45 in fin. ff. de usur.), namely with regard to natural equity. For by strict law he makes his own only the fruits consumed, and surviving fruits can be claimed by the true owner by the office of the judge (l. certum C. de rei vindic.); but pending fruits he does not make his own in the same way, because they are regarded as part of the field. Saxon law settles all these matters by two axioms, of which the first is as follows: one who cultivates another's field in good faith gains the fruits; in bad faith he loses both the fruits and his labour (gloss; Landrecht lib. 2 art. 46).
