units.tr: The second axiom is this: "What the harrow has passed over and the hoe has covered belongs to the heir of the sower" (Landrecht lib. 2 art. 58 & lib. 3 art. 76). As regards building, the following holds: the building and the material consumed in building also become the property of the owner of the soil. (1) If someone builds on his own soil with his own material (d. l. eo § si quis ff. ad exhibend.); (2) if he builds on his own soil with another's material (§ cum in suo Inst. de rer. div.; l. 1 & 2 ff. de superficiebus; l. 2 C. de rei vindic.); (3) if he builds on another's soil with his own material (l. planè ff. de petit. haered.; § ex diverso, d. doc.); (4) if he builds on another's soil with another's material (l. 2 C. de rei vindic.). It is not unreasonably asked here whether a building erected upon another's wall is acquired by the owner of the wall. We will defend the affirmative with Harpprecht (disp. 12 th. 1, in notes). The § cum in suo Inst. de rer. div. seems to stand in the way, but the answer is that the building is joined to the soil through the wall. The l. quemadmodum 29 § 1 ff. ad L. Aquil. also seems to stand in the way. The answer is, first, that a projection is so extended that it rests nowhere (l. malum 242 § 1 ff. de V.S.), and therefore it is not rightly said to be joined to the soil by means of a wall; second, that this happens on account of the nature of the servitude, for a projection is a kind of servitude (Coras. ad tit. ff. de damno infecto). Yet in order that the owner of the soil or of the wall acquire ownership of a building erected above, it is required, first, that the soil be private (d. § cum in suo Inst. de rer. div.). For on public soil, or soil common to all, the building does not go to the soil, but the soil goes to the building (l. in tantum 6 in pr. ff. de rer. div.; l. quod in litore 14 ff. de acquir. rer. dom.). Second, it is required that the thing built upon be immovable (l. 7 § 6 in suo ff. de acquir. rer. dom.). For acquisition by building does not hold in a movable thing (Titius 60 ff. eod.). If these two conditions are present, the owner of the soil becomes owner of the building to such an extent that the alien material joined to the building can be claimed neither by the action for recovery nor by the action for production (l. 23 § penult.; Julian 37 ff. de rei vindic.; § all. cum in suo; l. 7 § 10 ff. de acquir. rer. dom.), on account of the prohibition of the Twelve Tables, by which buildings must not be disfigured by removing a beam (tignum), that is, any material which is added to the structure of a building (l. 7 in pr. ff. ad exhibend.; § eum in suo Inst. de rer. div.; l. 1 ff. de tigno iuncto; l. tigni ff. de V.S.). Nevertheless the owner does not thereby cease to be owner (all. § cum in suo; l. eum qui 23 ff. de usurp.; l. 4 in rem; l. 3 in pr. ff. de rei vindic.). For in the second case, if the builder is a possessor of the material in good faith while the material's owner remains, the owner of the material has a praetorian action in factum for the single value, as in the action in rem (d. l. 1 in rem actio § dicit ff. de rei vind.; l. 98 in fin. ff. de solut.), and the action de tigno iuncto to recover double the value (all. § cum in suo; l. 1 ff. de tigno iuncto), and, if the building is demolished, he has not recovered double, the action for recovery of the thing and the action for production (all. § cum in suo; d. l. 7 § 10 in pr.; d. l. 1 & 2 ff. de tigno iuncto). But if the possessor of the material is in bad faith, the owner of the material who builds has against him the action de tigno iuncto for double the interest (l. in rem actio § tignum ff. de rei vindic.; l. 3 § sciendum ff. ad exhib.); and besides these actions, the condiction for theft if he bought it from a possessor in bad faith, and the action of theft if the builder himself took away that material (second case; gloss on l. 1 ff. de tigno iuncto). In the third case, however, the owner of the material, if he himself possesses the soil from the true owner, or if he builds in good faith, that is, unknowingly, with his own material on another's soil, being in possession of the building, can recover the expenses and the value of the material from the owner of the soil by retaining the building (fundam. l. si in arca 33 ff. de condict. indeb.; l. 48 (sumptus) ff. de rei vind.; l. in fundo 38 ff. de rei vindic.); but if he has neglected this interest, he can by an exception of fraud remove the owner from acquiring the building (§ all. ex diverso; l. 14 ff. de except. doli). But one who is not in possession of the building, if he has handed over the field and the building without deduction of expenses through error, can recover his own only by seeking the judge's aid, as Fomann thinks (d. disp. 9 th. 17 lit. C; fund. pro all. l. si in arca). This does not stand in the way of l. qui exceptionem 40 § si pars ff. de condict. indeb., or of l. heres 21 ff. ad Trebell., for they speak of the case where something is done and contracted between the one paying and the one receiving. By Saxon law, a tenant who has the usufruct, or another who possesses another's estate, may remove the buildings if the owner of the land refuses to restore the expenses of the building (Cantor, lib. 2 art. 53).

Loquitur enim de coreaceis, cereis, lapideis, ligneis tabulis quæ scribendæ delineandæ & vulgariter depingendæ rei gratiâ factæ sunt. Cajus verò in d.l.qua ratione de pictura artificiosa loquitur, alioquin sibi contrarius esset lib.2.Instit.b.tit.§.item 4. qualiter hosce text.consentiat Gœdd.d.loc.n.13.(g) In hoc acquisitionis modo scriptura charta cedit l.in rem 23.§.2.ff.de rei vind.l.3.§.penult, ff, ad exhib. §.lite-
units.tr: Fuarius[?], or another person who possesses land belonging to someone else, may remove the buildings if the owner of the soil refuses to repay the cost of the building. Cantor, bk. 2, arc. 53. But if he builds on another's soil in bad faith, that is, knowing that the soil belongs to another, he is presumed to have given the material away, and he loses it (arg. l. per errorem ff. de R.I., all. §. ex diverso). So far that, even after the building is demolished, he cannot claim it (all. §. 1, §. 2, C. de rei vind.; l. fi is contra quem C. de aedif. priv.), nor could he bring any action or exception of fraud (Schne. ad cum non solo, Instit. de rer. div.). It is seen to stand in the way (l. 2, C. de rei vind.), according to the opinion of Hottomanus, as cited by Donellus, bk. 4 comm., c. 33. And finally, fourthly, in the case where the material of a building must be paid by the owner of the soil, whether the builder was in good faith or in bad faith, and that payment has not been made while the building stands, the material may be claimed once the building is demolished (l. 2, C. de rei vind.). (c) In weaving, the woven thing goes to the one to whom it is woven (§. 26, Instit. de rer. div.), and it becomes a formal part of it (Gœd. ad l. Labeo ff. de U.S.). So purple woven into a cloak, or a thread woven into it, goes to the cloak, and becomes the property of the one whose cloak it was (l. 23, §. 3, ff. de rei vind.; l. tigni 7 ff. ad exh.), since it also loses its form and is so joined to the cloak that it becomes a formal part and cannot be separated (Gœ. d. loc.). (f) In this, the picture goes to the panel, and the panel becomes the property of the one whose picture it is (l. qua ratione 9, §. 2, ff. de acqu. rer. dom.; §. fi quis, Instit. de rer. div.), because the picture is not a simple addition to the panel, but an accessory which, by the specification of the panel, adds a form, so that it is no longer called a panel but a picture and an image (Gœdd. d. loc.; Foman. disp. 9, th. 25). Nor does Paul in l. in rem 23, §. sed et id 3, ff. de rei vind. stand in our way. For he speaks of tablets of leather, wax, stone or wood, made for writing, drawing and, in common usage, for painting. Gaius, however, in the said l. qua ratione, speaks of skilled painting; otherwise he would contradict himself, bk. 2, Instit., this title, §. item 4. In what way those texts agree is shown by Gœddaeus, loc. cit., n. 13. units.la: §. litera Instit. de rer. div. eo quod non fiat pars formalis charta Coed. d. loc. Mynsing putat olim propterea scripturam chartæ cessisse, quod charta olim in maximo fuerit pretio: Id vero hodie cum non in tanto pretio sit non similiter obtinere. Resp. vid. apud Foman. d. disp. 9. th. 23.
units.tr: §. littera, Instit. de rer. div., because the writing does not become a formal part of the paper (Coed. d. loc.). Mynsinger thinks that writing used to go to the paper for this reason, that paper was once held in very high value; but since it is not now held in such high value, the same rule does not hold. Reply: see Foman., d. disp. 9, th. 23.
